speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, March 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. E. W. George for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Fair, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Bryce.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I had agreed with the recent statement by the
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that governments had no philosopher's stone by which they could solve all the problems of the world, political and social. At the same time I was deploring the fact that there has been a tendency on the part of this government to promote the idea that all the wonderful progress and economic benefits we have seen in Canada since the war have been directly associated with the administrative policies of this government. Of course you cannot have it both ways, and today we find that we are faced with some real problems that have been outlined in the motion proposed by this party.
When I concluded my remarks last evening I was dealing specifically with farm problems, which have been discussed at some length already this session. I would point out that the dairy industry continues to decline. There is also a decline in diversified farming. In making their presentations to me many farmers declare that this decline in diversified farming, with all the harmful consequences it is bound to have on this basic industry, is the result of the income tax policy of this government, particularly as it applies to farmers in the prairie provinces. They feel it is of no personal benefit if they continue to produce beyond a certain level of income, because all the results of their endeavours will be skimmed off by the excessive income tax. Of course the problem of labour supply is associated with that condition as well. Last evening it was pointed out by the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) that there is a severe lack of qualified recruits for our agricultural industry. He told us that since the end of the war 77 per cent of all immigrants have found their way to the industrialized east rather than to the area of Canada most in need of these human resources. These difficulties are giving rise to a new agrarian protest which is making itself felt on the prairies. I am sure that this agrarian protest, which in the last thirty years has produced two great political movements, with their consequent divisive effect on Canadian unity would be much more severe today were it not for the fact that we have been blessed with an unbroken series of good crops and relatively stable prices due to prevailing world shortages.
This leads me to the conclusion that in the west we have never subscribed to the myth that has been so carefully cultivated by our government, that all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds. As I listen to the representatives from the maritimes I feel that they too have much the same attitude. Highlighting the situation so far as we are concerned is the redistribution bill which
302	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale was introduced yesterday, and which indicates that Saskatchewan and Manitoba are both faced with the loss of several representatives in this house. I have some statistics on the population decline in the prairies published by the Manitoba defence development committee. This committee outlines the situation as follows:
As evidence of this the population of the prairie provinces in 1941 was 2,422,000, but during the next five years, due in great part to this migration, the population dropped 59,000, a decrease of 2-4 per cent. From 1946 to 1951, when this drain was not present, the prairie provinces increased their population by 175,000. It is a reasonable assumption that the need for industrial workers in the central provinces cost the prairies over 200,000 persons during the war years.
Those figures will become significant as in a few moments I proceed to deal with the problem of industrialization on the prairies.
Related to the redistribution situation, however, we have the matter of federal aid to education. For years now, due to this rural-urban migration carrying off the cream of our young people, we have been subsidizing the east educationally. As soon as our young people graduate from high school, rather than making their contribution on the prairies they move to the central provinces of Ontario or Quebec in search of employment. At the basis of this problem is the factor of the slow industrial development of the prairies. Actually we are just beginning to industrialize. Recent reports, particularly since the war, are very encouraging. For example, we can boast that during 1951 our gross product in Manitoba amounted to $546 million, and the number of workers now employed in Manitoba industry total 44,700, which is an increase of 87 per cent.
On the prairies we are just beginning to move toward a diversified economy. Perhaps we are in the same position that Ontario and Quebec found themselves in at the close of world war I. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the only permanent solution for the repeated expression of agrarian protest with which we have been faced during the first half of the twentieth century is to have a diversified economy. It seems to me that the fact that we are today faced with a tremendous task in defence production provides an excellent opportunity to encourage the industrial trend that is already under way on the iprairies. Other encouraging factors are the recent discovery of oil in Manitoba, in two parts of my own- riding, one near the town of Virden, and the other near the town of Reston; and the mining developments in the northern part of the province. I say that with the huge contracts being awarded in connection with defence production, we have


an opportunity of encouraging the trend that is already so substantially under way in Manitoba.
If we examine the situation up to the present time, we are forced to the conclusion that there has been no real effort in this regard. In an article in Saturday Night last autumn, prepared by the editor of the Winnipeg Tribune, this title was used: "Manitoba ready and waiting." Recent statistics released by the Manitoba defence development committee express the situation in more concrete terms. The committee states:
With 5'7 per cent of Canada's population and 4 per cent of Canada's manufacturing capacity, Manitoba to date (January 15, 1952) has received 2-8 per cent of the money spent in defence contracts. Of this 2-8 per cent approximately one third has been for the construction of air stations and other military establishments, which, while helpful, have no peacetime industrial value. Furthermore, of the remaining contracts placed here a substantial portion are for clothing and for aircraft work of which a high proportion of the total cost represents materials, parts, engines, etc., which were manufactured in the central provinces.
I was delighted to read in a report of the defence production board for February that Brandon had received its first real defence contract. Recorded on page 3 of that publication was the information that a contract had been awarded to the Canadian Brown Steel Tank Company for the sum of approximately $140,000. There was only one sour note in that announcement, in that they listed Brandon as Brandon, Ontario, instead of Brandon, Manitoba. I can only conclude this error was due to force of habit.
I must now conclude my remarks. The members from the west, as well as the members from other parts of Canada, gave their wholehearted support to the St. Lawrence seaway project when it was before us last session. We did so realizing that the immediate effect of the St. Lawrence project would1 be to intensify the centralization of industry in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. We understood, however, that it was important to the defence of Canada, and all we ask is that, in the total industrial development of Canada, a conscious program of national development be undertaken by the government for the development of a healthy national life.
I think we are forced to the conclusion that there has never been a time in the history of Canada when centralization has proceeded more rapidly than it has during the past dozen years. If we are to have an equitable distribution of population, to maintain the basis of Canadian unity and to prepare in this country the bulwarks of defence, we must realize that a basic consideration should be the dispersal of industry right

across the country, the allotment of defence contracts in such a way that the minimum of disturbance is introduced into the economy, and making sure that this work is handled in the most economical way possible, with an eye to the future as well as the urgent demands of the immediate.
I am sorry that my time is exhausted, Mr. Speaker. I have more to say, but there will be other opportunities to take part in further discussions.

Mr. Speaker, I first wish to offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. To us who come from New Brunswick the excellence of the speech made by the mover was not surprising, because he is one of our colleagues. He performed his task in an extraordinarily capable manner, and, with the hon. member for Lake St. John, is deserving of the highest commendation.
It was with satisfaction that we learned from the speech from the throne that at this session of parliament a bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act is to be introduced. I sincerely hope that this bill is being designed to provide for general increases in the rates payable to veterans who come within the scope of this act. I further hope that those increases, if they come, will be in keeping with the spirit of the act and will provide for the recipients of the allowance and their dependents sufficient funds to enable them to maintain their independence and their self-respect.
No one will deny the principle of these allowances. It is one that has been recognized for many years by national leaders, by governments and by citizens generally in this country. I refer to the principle that special assistance is owing by the state to those of our countrymen whose minds or bodies have become ravaged through wartime service in the uniform of their sovereign. Having in mind the fact that this principle has been accepted, it is the solemn duty of parliament to regulate the rates of this special assistance in order to meet the exigencies of the times. I have had personal contact with many of these cases and have firsthand knowledge whereof I speak. I am particularly concerned about cases in which children are involved, believing as I do that a special formula of rates should be devised so that those children may be provided for in a normal manner.
I express particular concern over these cases, but I also express concern over another matter. When the increases are forthcoming,
The Address-Mr. Riley it is to be hoped that the maximum extra income, beyond the assistance, allowed under the act will also be increased. While I am on the subject I should also like to point out that more discretion should be allowed to the war veterans allowance board, or more leniency should be shown by them, in consideration and examination of applications from widows of war veterans for special assistance.
The main subject, Mr. Speaker, of my remarks today is the condition now existing in the port of Saint John. From time to time, more particularly in recent years, the facilities of the port of Saint John have been taxed up to and beyond their limits. Since the disastrous fire which destroyed most of our port's facilities back in 1931 there has been a gradual rebuilding of the piers and sheds along our waterfront. But with this rebuilding has also come an increase in the amount of traffic which flows into and out of our port. The port of Saint John is one of the two ports available for winter traffic on the Atlantic seaboard of this country. Because of that fact, our port and the port of Halifax occupy a vitally strategic position in the economy of the country. At the present time we have in Saint John berthage for twenty-four deep-sea vessels and two coastal vessels. We have something like ten piers on the one side of the harbour, or ten main wharves, and a couple on the east side. Over the past ten years we have had something like 33 million tons of freight go through our port. During the past year this traffic has tended to increase more than ever. Because of this fact I want to focus the attention of the membership of this house on our port today.
Over the past week or so I have received a large number of complaints from businessmen, from the mayor of the city of Saint John, and from the president and members of our board of trade. These complaints deal with the fact that our port is overcrowded at the present time. As I said, we have something like twenty-four berths for deep-sea vessels. When I received some complaints last week about a number of vessels lying outside of the berths at anchor, I checked on the matter and at that time I found that there were thirty-five vessels in port. Twenty-one of them were working, six were at anchor, five were awaiting berths and three were under repair. The complaints last week dealt mainly with the fact that some of the pit-prop exports which were leaving our province were held up, or that the ships which were going to load those pit-props were held up. I investigated and found that on this particular occasion, because rail traffic had been

The Address-Mr. Riley handicapped by heavy snowstorms in the eastern provinces, and because there may have been some mutual understanding between port authorities and the shippers, these pit-props were not being handled as expeditiously as they might have been. There may be a very good explanation for this condition, but it arose at a time when the port was congested otherwise, and it sharply focused the attention not only of our businessmen and citizens generally in the city of Saint John, but also of our provincial authorities, on this particular problem which had to do with the export and import traffic through our harbour. .
The question may be raised as to why those who have nothing to do with the operation of our harbour itself may become interested in what might appear to be trifling problems of this nature. But I want to point out that the port of Saint John constitutes an integral part of the economy of our province and a very important part of the economy of the country. It should also be borne in mind that, unlike the port of Montreal, the citizens generally in the city of Saint John are seriously affected by problems which affect the port. We have something like 5,000 waterfront workers whose livelihood depends largely upon the movement of freight through our port. I can quite understand the reasons why our citizens have become aroused over the fact that the facilities available at Saint John harbour at the present time are insufficient to handle the amount of freight which is now going through the different docks.
I have wondered at times whether in requesting the construction of other facilities in our harbour I might not be shouting against the wind. I have wondered whether the volume of traffic generally throughout the year would not warrant the huge capital expenditures which are necessary on the part of the federal treasury in order to provide additional berths in a harbour such as ours. But after talking to shipping people, speaking to shipping agents and hearing accounts of the diversion, because of the lack of facilities, of ships which might otherwise have come to Saint John, I have come to the conclusion that we have reached the stage where we must demand more forcibly that additional port facilities be made available along our harbour front.
I have had occasion to bring to the attention of the cabinet the fact that we should have a continuous program of port expansion, and in recent years I have been advised that port expansion programs must necessarily be curtailed because of the necessity of


heavy defence expenditures. Well, I maintain that the expenditure of capital funds in expanding port facilities in ports such as we have in Saint John and Halifax go away beyond national defence requirements. They are an integral part of the economy of the country, and as the economy of Canada expands, as our trade expands, we must be in a position to handle the incoming and outgoing traffic through our ports.
I have reference at this time particularly to a couple of dilapidated docks on the east side of our harbour, which should constitute the next step in the rebuilding program of our port. The Digby boat wharf, so-called, and the Reeds Point wharf, are in such a dilapidated condition that they are not only a disgrace to our city but a disgrace to this country as a whole. I know that there have been instances in which ships would have come to use the facilities of our port if these particular berths were available and in shape for ocean-going vessels. When I was down in Saint John last year with some fifty members of parliament I had occasion to point out to them, standing on Pugsley pier-the newest of our piers on the eastern side of the harbour-the appallingly dilapidated condition of the Digby boat wharf. I have a picture in my hand which was enlarged from a snapshot taken by one of the visitors at that time. It shows that I am pointing out to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford) the disgraceful condition of this pier. I recall that at that time he expressed concern over it. In a port such as we have in Saint John we should keep pace with our expanding commerce and have these berths available for the type of traffic offered. I can remember at that time that the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Blue) expressing somewhat similar sentiments, and also the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing). The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) expressed the same sentiments. Therefore when I bring this problem to the attention of the house I bring it to the attention of men who have had some firsthand knowledge of the conditions existing in our harbour.
I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) is aware of these conditions. I know that during personal tours of inspection of our harbour front he has expressed some concern himself over the condition of the Digby boat wharf and the Reeds Point wharf. At the same time I know that the Minister of Transport-although he is deeply sympathetic and wants to see the facilities of these ports expand; I feel certain of that-does not make government policy. It is for this reason that I want to urge upon the government as a whole that they allocate sufficient funds to rebuild the Digby boat wharf and the Reeds

Point wharf. Although it may cost millions of dollars, and the defence program may be such that public works of a non-essential character should be curtailed, I want to see the government allocate sufficient funds to rebuild these piers, because they are as essential as most defence projects, and tie in directly with them.
I further think that the rebuilding of these piers should be but the commencement of a continued and uninterrupted program of expansion of the port of Saint John. The long wharf which lies to the east side of the harbour is in such a disgraceful dilapidated condition that it needs but a nudge to collapse into the water. We need an extension of some of the piers on the west side of the harbour. We need new berths beyond the ones I have mentioned on the east side of the harbour, and we need some development work in the Courtenay bay area.
These may seem to be extravagant demands for my constituency, but if the government will examine the significance of the necessity for these expenditures I am sure that they will agree with me that they constitute the type of expenditure which should be made at this time.
I should like to mention also the question of the defence of Saint John harbour. During the last war when we had to defend our coast line there were a number of unfortunate sinkings in the area of Halifax. We know that submarines were hovering off the coast at times when the lifeline of the allied nations was in need of careful preservation. Because of a lack of harbour facilities at Saint John it was necessary at times for seven or eight ships to lie at anchor and thus provide perfect targets for submarines. It is only by pure luck that we did not have sinkings directly outside of Saint John harbour.
This may sound like an extravagant statement, but I think the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) will bear me out when I say that at a time when we were feeling comfortably secure along the Atlantic coast an enemy submarine landed a human cargo just a few miles southeast of the harbour of Saint John. At that particular time there must have been seven or eight ships strung out within a few miles of the landing point of that submarine. I feel sure that the only reason' that torpedoes were not launched at those ships was that the captain of the enemy submarine had been given orders to land his human cargo and get out of the way without exciting undue apprehension on the part of those in charge of that defence area.
The main section of Saint John is located on a peninsula and there are only two narrow arteries, with bridges on each, leading from
The Address-Mr. Riley the city. It would be quite possible to cripple those bridges with small charges of explosives. I do not know the defence program in connection with our east coast ports and it may well be that provision for the necessary protection has been made, but in case it has not, I urge upon the government the necessity of paying particular attention to the port of Saint John and perhaps to the port of Halifax as well. This matter may be within the scope of civil defence and if so I hope they will take heed of what I am saying. It may be considered a municipal responsibility, but when regard is given to the fact that Saint John is a vital and strategic port in time of war and in time of peace the problem becomes national in scope.
When we urge the necessity of defence in the Saint John area we do not do so simply for the security of our own families and our own property; we do it because we feel there is a need for national security. Before I close I want to urge that something be done in the immediate future to correct this serious situation which presently exists in Saint John harbour, due to the fact that there are not sufficient port facilities to handle the ever-increasing volume of traffic going through that port. In order to show that this traffic is increasing, I should like to indicate the tonnage handled in certain months last year as well as in certain months this year. The figures are as follows:

It will be seen that the increase is substantial. I should like to stress again the possibilities of loss of traffic. On Friday of last week I was informed by some of my shipping friends in Saint John that two ships had left the harbour because they could not wait either to load or to unload their cargoes. I do not know where those ships went; they may have gone to the United States or over to Halifax.

Mr. Speaker, it was towards the latter part of the morning that I found I might have an opportunity to say a few words this afternoon. Since that time I was invited to a luncheon provided by the Canadian Horticultural Council and, having arrived here somewhat after three o'clock, have had to make a few hasty notes. After the excellent luncheon provided by these kind gentlemen, I might say that I am not in a particularly good condition to speak at length, but I will have to do the best I can.
First of all I want to express my complete support for the very logical and well-documented point of view on foreign affairs presented to the house by our leader when speaking in this debate. I am not going to add at any length to the excellent case he made for our point of view, but I think the views he presented to the house are supported by far more people in Canada than some hon. members realize. We in this group

are for the Atlantic defence policy. We support rearmament for defence. We support collective security amongst democrats for defence. We are opposed to association with former nazis or fascists in order to defend democracy.
There are sound reasons for a good many of us viewing with some alarm the situation that has developed with respect to western defence and negotiations aiming towards peace in Korea. The things that disturb us are not the policies announced by the United States government or the policies of other responsible people but the statements made by people in non-political circles in the United States or those who are playing a very important part in the economies of other countries in which they live. I want to illustrate that point by reading one or two comments from newspapers. I refer first to the Ottawa Citizen of March 10 and particularly to an Associated Press dispatch from Washington which reads as follows:
United States policy makers are fighting persistent arguments of a "war now!" group which believes the United States should launch a sudden attack on red Russia in an all-out war to destroy communism.
United States policy makers are doing that, Mr. Speaker, and we are of the opinion that members of this house should get up and support these people who are trying to down those who are declaring for a policy of allout war now. The article continues:
For more than a year there have been clear signs that some military men and civilians are convinced war with Russia is inevitable and therefore the United States should strike first. Each time President Truman or his lieutenants have taken quick action to slap down this line of thinking. It runs directly counter to the administration's announced policy of trying to force an understanding with Russia without war.
But despite this opposition the war talk persists beneath the surface by those whose thinking goes like this:
"Russia is determined to dominate the world. When Russia is strong enough the red leaders will send their armies and those of their satellites against the western world. This war of conquest will come like Pearl Harbor-without warning. This being true, then the United States should strike first in a 'preventive war' to beat Russia to the punch."
In capsule form this is the situation now spotlighted by the diary of Major General Robert W. Grow which somehow was stolen from him by the communists last year. Grow wrote the diary while United States military attache in Moscow. The army says parts of the diary are being used in the red propaganda drive against the United States. One extract quoted Grow as writing:
"It seems to me the time is ripe for a blow this year . . . We must start by hitting below the belt. This war cannot be conducted by Marquis of Queensbury rules."
The viewpoint expressed in the diary recalls that in the summer of 1950 an air force general was rebuked for offering publicly to destroy Russia's

A-bomb centres. In this case Major General Orvil Anderson, then head of the air war college, gave an interview in which he was quoted:
"Give me the order to do it and I can break up Russia's five A-bomb nests in a week, and when I went up to Christ I think I could explain to Him that I had saved civilization."
A few days earlier the secretary of the navy, then Francis P. Matthews, had made a speech in which he said the United States should be ready if necessary to start a war to "compel co-operation for peace." The statement was disavowed by both the White House and the state department. But this line of thinking persists even though government and military leaders have rejected it time and again.
Our point in this group is that parliamentary leaders and governments throughout the world must have direct control over rearmament and defensive policies, and that there are great dangers to us and to other countries if these military people are allowed to express their opinions and influence others along these lines. I have checked the papers since the leader of our group presented our statement on foreign policy. I find that some papers seem to have misunderstood his statement, I presume because of not reading it carefully, and others support it. I should like to read an editorial appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of March 10. It is headed, "A Plea for Canadian Leadership", and I think it puts the case very well from our point of view. It reads as follows:
In the present state of international affairs many Canadians of all political persuasions will be inclined to agree with Mr. M. J. Coldwell, the C.C.F. leader, that Canada should take a stronger stand for constructive policies. Mr. Coldwell has suggested during the debate on the speech from the throne that Canada propose to its allies direct political negotiations to end the Korean war. He is alarmed by talk in the United States of promoting the spread of conflict with China, a policy that by crippling the west and consolidating communist regimes could prove disastrous. Mr. Coldwell thinks NATO has become over-ambitious militarily and should direct to underdeveloped areas some of the funds earmarked for weapons. It is certainly evident that in both Korea and western Europe policies conceived in military terms have not been politically successful. NATO's publicized plans for spending $300 million to equip about 90 divisions over the next three years are widely regarded as unrealistic and excessive even if feasible. Granted that adequate defensive strength must be achieved militarily, the fact remains that collective security requires vigorous social and economic exertions.
That is one great criticism this group has of developments to date under the Atlantic pact. We are now being told about what are termed by even conservative newspapers fantastic military propositions, while at the same time nothing has been done so far to implement article 2 of the Atlantic pact, which provides for economic assistance and so on.
As Prime Minister St. Laurent told the Canadian Federation of Agriculture last January, "the secure peace in the world which we all want" is in danger so long as great numbers of people are hungry. For education week, Mr. L. B. Pearson,
The Address-Mr. Herridge
the minister of external affairs, issued the message that "our defences must consist of ideas as well as weapons". Yet Canada expects to provide billions for armaments while apparently content with $25 million a year for a constructive program like the Colombo plan.
Politics, of course, entered into the military planning zeal of the recent north Atlantic council meeting at Lisbon-in particular the internal politics of the United States, where in an election year the administration desires at least the appearance of notable results of its foreign policy, and congress sharpens the economic axe. The NATO allies cannot disregard one another's domestic problems. But political thought and action on a much higher and broader plane will be needed if international relations are to be shrewdly managed so that conditions favourable to peace may be created.
I think the editor of that newspaper has written in a very statesmanlike way. Now I want to refer briefly to the Korean situation. In that connection I support what our leader had to say in this respect, and his remarks addressed to the leaders of the governments now carrying on the negotiations. I think the dangers of allowing these negotiations to be carried on by military people are evidenced by a Canadian Press dispatch from Seoul dated March 10, from which I am going to quote briefly to indicate the frame of mind of the military leaders and their inability to understand the point of view of their enemies and the thinking of the average man:
General James A. Van Fleet disclosed Saturday the Chinese and Korean reds have built up a force of about 900,000 men in Korea, but there is no indication of a spring offensive. The U.S. eighth army commander said in an interview the reds have more men, weapons and planes but that the allies have enough to stop any attack. He said about 450,000 reds are in the front lines.
Van Fleet added that he would be "surprised" if the communists attempted an offensive similar to their costly but unsuccessful major drives in April and May of last year.
"I am confident we could stop any attack the communists might throw at us," he said. "It would be a good thing if we could get those people out of their foxholes and dugouts to mow them down the way we did last April and May."
Just imagine the thinking of a man supposed to represent Christian nations, who apparently would welcome the opportunity to mow down his enemies as they did last April and May. A general speaking in those terms does not represent the thinking of the majority of the people who are backing the resistance to aggression in Korea. In my opinion it is disgraceful for a military commander of a nation supposed to be Christian to utter sentiments like those. Those of us who are sincere believe in opposing aggression, but we regret the loss of life incurred in doing so.

Yes, but we do not glory in it. He goes on:
"We still have an intense desire to do it. We have enough equipment, men and ammunition available. We could do it just as effectively as we did last year."
I bring to the attention of members of this house the frame of mind of a man like this, and ask what chance he has to carry on successful negotiations with a view to arranging an armistice and we hope finally peace. I mention these facts to illustrate to the house statements being made that cause serious concern not only to a group such as ours but to many Canadians. In my own constituency in addition to people who support the C.C.F. party there are a number of good citizens who are Liberals, and a number of citizens who support the Progressive Conservative party. I know some of them wholeheartedly endorse the statement made by my leader a few days ago with respect to foreign affairs.
That is all I am going to say on that point at this time, except to quote what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) had to say on this question during this debate, because I think in this paragraph at page 117 of Hansard the hon. member brought the whole subject into focus in a very few sentences:
It seems to us-
And when our leader says "us" he means the C.C.F. group in this house and our supporters in the country.
-that NATO has been influenced almost entirely by domestic and political considerations in the United States. This is an election year there. Most nations are dependent upon our great neighbour for financial and economic aid. Fortunately Canada* has paid her own way and is in no sense dependent on the United States for financial or economic aid. Hence we are in a peculiar position of being able in NATO, and indeed in the United Nations when necessary, to give a lead towards the acceptance of more sensible and constructive policies than we have been getting.
That is the point. This group believes this government is in a most favourable position to give a stronger lead than it has given in the past, and to offer more sensible and constructive policies with regard to foreign affairs, our rearmament for defence, and our resistance to aggression in Korea.
Now I want to speak in a more parochial vein; I think that is the term used by the writer for Saturday Night when members speak of things that directly concern their constituents, or matters of particular interest in their own constituency. During each recess, like all members of this group I usually get around my riding as much as possible, not only speaking to various organizations but meeting people. I like to go on the farms,


to go down in the mines, to go into the lumber camps and the smelters. I like to meet people who are working from day to day, to find out what they are really thinking about current problems in Canada. I have found that the people are anxious to discuss many matters with me, and a considerable number are interested in the few matters I am going to bring to the attention of the house now.
I had the opportunity to address a considerable number of branches of the Canadian Legion, and to talk to many widows, dependents and others interested in veterans questions. I found that thousands of veterans and veterans' dependents throughout this country are very interested in amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am very pleased that the government has indicated the intention to bring a measure before the house amending that act. The personal contacts I have had with hundreds of people and the correspondence I have received indicate very clearly the great and increasing need for something to be done for this large and needy segment of our population. Only two or three days ago I received a letter from a very fine lady in my constituency, the widow of a veteran who rendered great service to this country. She and her husband came to Canada some forty-five years ago with a little capital, and in this letter she retails her life history. She tells how their capital vanished in developing their little ranch; what they went through; how her husband went overseas, where he was wounded and gassed; how he spent some twenty-five or twenty-seven years in poor health and then died. She recounts the circumstances in which she finds herself today. In other words she writes a letter that thousands could write. When one talks to people in those circumstances, when one gets letters of that kind by the dozen, one realizes to the full the need for great improvements in the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am not going to say more about that at this time, Mr. Speaker, because when the bill comes before the house we shall have an opportunity of presenting our views. I hope the government goes further than the representatives of the Canadian Legion proposed during their last meeting with the cabinet.
Another thing I found that did concern many of the older people was something that was mentioned by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) yesterday. He does not miss very much, Mr. Speaker. He looks at the economic and social life of this country through a microscope, and then presents his findings to this house. The hon. member mentioned that he had found a number of old age pensioners who had been

drawing the old age pension prior to December 31, 1951, and who were quite concerned about recoveries against estates. I found exactly the same situation in my constituency. A number of people are quite uncertain as to what is going to happen. They have been receiving the pension for some years and have decided, in their own minds, that there is a lien against their property. I understand that there is some confusion as a result of the constitutional situation or as a result of an agreement between the federal and provincial governments. I feel that at this session the government ought to relieve those people's minds by washing out that aspect of any agreement.
There happen to be a number of superannuated civil servants in my constituency who have retired from public works, post office, customs and the other departments scattered throughout the district. I find that some of these superannuated civil servants are in needy circumstances. The member for Winnipeg North Centre said yesterday that there were 1,478 superannuated civil servants who were receiving less than $40 per month. There were 2,647 widows of civil servants who were receiving less than $40 a month. I trust that the government will listen to the very eloquent plea of the member for Winnipeg North Centre, and do something at this session to relieve those people from their necessitous condition.
Like other members in this group, I regret that there is no provision being made this year for the establishment of a committee to study a national health plan. Members would be surprised to find the growing interest and demand for some form of national health program. As a result of the experience in the provincial field it has been found that, regardless of the best the provincial governments can do because of their limited facilities and circumstances, we are not going to have satisfactory health or medical services in this country until they are correlated, within the framework of a national health program.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I certainly support the subamendment moved by the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), urging the government to take action with respect to stabilizing prices to protect the producers and consumers. Just prior to coming into this chamber at three o'clock I had a discussion with a number of people from British Columbia who told my colleague the member for Yale (Mr. Jones) and myself that a considerable increase in the price of meat in British Columbia had already taken place. This is only the beginning. If it is found necessary to maintain this ban on the movement of meat from one province to the other,
The Address-Mr. Herridge the situation is going to become quite serious.
I urge the government to give consideration to the proposal contained in the amendment moved by the member for Selkirk.
Before I conclude I want to deal with a few matters of direct interest to the riding I have the honour to represent. For the information of some of the prairie members who are not so fortunate as to live in as fine a part of the country as I do, may I say that the greater part of the Columbia river community, as we call it, is within my constituency. The Columbia river community is that part of Canada the history of which, when future history is written, will be written in the terms of the history of the Nile, the Mississippi and the other great rivers of the world.
The Columbia river basin is an area of 39,000 square miles in Canada, rich in land, timber, minerals and water power resources.
I intend to be brief, but wish to give some indication of the tremendous developments in this district-I am glad the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is listening because I have an appeal to make to him later. I shall outline a few of the developments. I speak with some sentiment on the matter because I come from a family that has lived in that district nearly fifty years, and has waited nearly fifty years to see the things happening that are happening today. I am very glad that we had faith enough to wait that time. At the junction of the Columbia and Waneta rivers there is a dam and power plant being erected that will cost over $30 million. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company is spending something in the nature of $10 million on the expansion of its Trail plants. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and the West Kootenay Power and Light Company are spending something over $5 million in power line extension to Kimberley and to the mine at Riondel. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is some time since I have taken the opportunity of saying a word in the debate on the speech from the throne. Today I do so for a very special reason.
On December 3 last, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) asked me if I was going to make a statement at an early date concerning the progress of negotiations with the United States and Japan with respect to the fisheries treaty. At that time the officials had not completed drafting the agreement nor had it been brought to the attention of my colleagues. I therefore did not feel that it was the proper time for me to make any report. I gave an undertaking to the hon. member that I would report to this house as soon as possible after receiving the completed draft and after discussing it with my colleagues.
Although the agreement was tabled on December 29, this is the first occasion when it seemed appropriate for me to make a report regarding the treaty. I am pleased to do so now.
I would very much like to follow the usual courtesies and extend my congratulations to the constituencies of Westmorland and Lake St. John as well as to the two members representing those ridings who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This house always recognizes industry, ability and efficiency; it also recognizes quite readily the marks of a gentleman which were so evident in these two members and in their speeches. They gave the historical background of their ridings, what they had accomplished to date and what they hoped they might do, making it clear that these two links in the chain of confederation are healthy, sound, and ready to play their parts in the development of Canada. These encouraging words are appreciated by all members of the house.

I now want to say something about the United States-Japan-Canada tripartite agreement on fisheries.
For some time it was thought that there would be something in the peace treaty with Japan referring to fisheries, not only on the west coast of Canada, but in other parts of the Pacific as well. Early in the spring of 1951, the deputy minister, Mr. Stewart Bates, and I were invited to Washington to discuss with Mr. John Foster Dulles this problem. Soon after we met him and began talking about the problem we were convinced that an attempt to include a fishery agreement in the peace treaty itself would mean endless work and delay. It would mean a separate agreement between Japan and all our allies, particularly in the Pacific. We were convinced after our talk with Mr. Dulles that he was right and that our best plan was to work out a separate fisheries agreement. Again after a great deal of consideration and after discussing it with the fishing industry and fishermen of the west coast, it was thought that a tripartite agreement with Japan and the United States and Canada was the only really sensible sort of agreement. His Excellency the prime minister of Japan had already indicated by letter to Mr. Dulles that he would enter into a fisheries agreement with us and other nations promptly after the signing of the main peace treaty.
The prime minister of Japan, during a brief visit with my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and myself at San Francisco, asked us if we would be prepared to go to Tokyo shortly to discuss such an agreement. We assured him that we would be ready. An official invitation was extended to us in October last. After that and before leaving for Japan we had further discussions with the fishermen and with the industry. The Canadian delegation to Tokyo consisted of the deputy minister of the Department of Fisheries, Mr. Sam Ozere, legal counsel to the department, my colleague Mr. E. T. Applewhaite, member for Skeena, Dr. J. L. Hart, head of the biological station at Nanaimo, Mr. John Buchanan, representing the industry of British Columbia, and myself.
I think it is advisable for me at this point to indicate why an agreement of any sort was necessary. Those living on the Pacific coast have for a good many years been very deeply concerned about the danger of Japanese fishermen coming to British Columbia to fish our salmon, halibut and herring. The Japanese expedition to Bristol bay before the war demonstrated that this was possible and that they were actually thinking along this line.

This trip also created a great deal of resentment against the Japanese fishermen. While the Japanese fishermen had never fished along our coast, yet there was no reason why they could not, and very sound reasons as to why they would do it. For many years Japan has been the leading country in the world as far as fisheries are concerned, taking first place in the volume of her catch before the second world war. In addition to that, Japan needs what she gets from the sea to feed her people, probably more than any other nation. I understand that about eighty per cent of her protein is harvested from the sea. She also needs some of the other valuable species such as salmon and tuna for export purposes, and her fisheries have been considerably reduced as a result of the recent war, since Russia is now in command of the very valuable salmon fisheries formerly enjoyed by her. It was therefore necessary, if we wanted to add stability and security to the fishing industry on the British Columbia coast, to make some agreement with Japan.
The basis of this agreement involved two questions of principle which were difficult to reconcile: the right of all nations to the freedom of the seas and the reverse of that, to restrict Japan from fishing near Canadian or American shores. However, the solution to the problem was readily available. Canada and the United States both have a long history of conservation of certain species- salmon, halibut and herring- and it is quite true to say that these fisheries would probably have been lost to the world's food supply had we not over the years taken very rigid conservation methods. For many years we have restricted our fishermen as to the time they could commence seasonal fishing, when they would cease fishing, restricting all fishing for two or three days a week, regulating the length of their nets and the size of the mesh, and on many occasions leaving idle fishing gear and plants while these regulations were being applied. In addition to that, the government of Canada has spent large sums of money year after year for the scientific study of these species. Industries locating on our rivers were obliged to prevent pollution and to construct, at their own expense, dams and fishways to meet our regulations in order to provide easy ascent to the spawning grounds and safety in the spawning grounds. Likewise, the taxpayers of Canada have paid for both river and sea patrols to see that these regulations were carried out. We have also made international agreements between the United States and Canada for the conservation and propagation of the sockeye salmon on
The Address-Mr. Mayhew the Fraser river as well as for the halibut fishery, so that Canada as a whole, and the fishermen and fishing industry of British Columbia in particular, had a capital investment in the three species-salmon, halibut and herring. The fact that we had been doing this work for years made it comparatively easy and gave us a reasonable argument to use with Japan as to why they should waive their rights, not to the freedom of the high seas, but to fish these species in the waters of the east Pacific.
In gaining this concession, we obtained for the fishing industry of British Columbia what it has been most anxious to obtain and what it has been insisting on for some years. It was obtained not as a punitive measure nor because Japan was a defeated nation. It was obtained because it was a reasonable and1 fair request to make, one that in the same circumstances we would be ready to grant to any other nation in the Pacific.
Some of those who are opposing this agreement, and I believe others who are not opposing it but have not given it very serious consideration have asked the question, and I might say we have asked1 the question ourselves-why not just a simple agreement between Japan and Canada, each agreeing not to fish within a certain radius or area of each other's shore line? That sounds very simple and I am sure quite reasonable to a lot of people. But I would ask you to take just a second look at it. If you do you will see that such an agreement would mean the zoning of the Pacific ocean. Both Japan and ourselves would have to enter into separate agreements with other nations on a similar basis, and what would be the result? While I was travelling from Seoul to Tokyo by plane, the navigator had a map on his desk, and I asked him if he could give me roughly the coast line of Japan in miles as compared to the Canadian coast line; with the coast line of Japan, I included the inland sea of Japan. In a very few minutes, he was able to give me the approximate mileage. You would probably be surprised1 to know that the mileage of the coast line of Japan is approximately five times that of the coast line of British Columbia from point to point. If the whole of the Pacific area was divided up as suggested, Canada would suffer since she has one of the shortest shore lines of any country in the Pacific basin.
Others claim that this is by no means a perfect agreement as far as Canada and the United States are concerned. With that we agree, because it is not an agreement with the United States at all. It has not changed our relationship with the United States and we enjoy all the rights and privileges that

The Address-Mr. Mayhew we have ever had with that country. This is expressly stated in our agreement, and in this agreement we used the same wording as was used previously in the convention tor the northwest Atlantic fisheries. I quote:
Nothing in this convention shall he deemed to affect adversely the claims ot any contracting party in regard to the limits of territorial waters or to the jurisdiction of a coastal state over fisheries.
We have made no concession whatever to the United States.
However, the United States and Japan realized and so stated that the stocks of fish on the North American coast are so intermingled that it would be impossible to segregate them in any way that would be practical of administration. Therefore the conference agreed that under no condition would Canada and the United States be asked to abstain from fishing any species of fish from and including the gulf of Alaska southward to the gulf of Mexico. That is a recognition which is very valuable to the Canadian fisherman.
We do agree not to fish for red salmon in the Bristol bay area. The United States claims that there is no intermingling of this stock of fish with others along our coast or the coast of Asia. If that is proven by the commission which is being set up as a judicial body, not as a regulatory body, then we will permanently, or as long as this agreement lasts, not fish for red salmon in that area. But if the commission proves that there is an intermingling of these stocks of fish, then, because it would come under the principles which we applied in making this agreement, we will be free if we wish to fish in these waters. In the meantime we have the right, if we wish to use it, to fish any other species in the Behring sea, and to fish for salmon west of the 175th meridian.
Another complaint that is sometimes heard is that this is a five-year agreement. It is a five-year agreement if we cease to carry on with the conservation methods and management techniques that we have employed for years, but if we continue to employ, as I am sure we will, these same protections, then the agreement will last for ten years or indefinitely.
Another point that is brought up is that we have extended an invitation to Japan to fish for cod, flounders and other groundfish along our coast. That of course is very, very far from the truth. Japan, or any other nation that cares to, may fish outside the three-mile limit of our coast or the coast line of any other country. But Japan has never found it worth while to cross the Pacific nearly 6,000 miles to fish for the species just mentioned,

and I do not believe that she will do so now since she has waived her right to fish salmon, halibut and herring.
In this agreement we have established a principle that can easily be applied to a fourth, fifth or any other number of nations that want to accept it. I cannot say that this has been secured without cost. It has been secured at the cost of many millions of dollars, the millions of dollars which we have spent in conservation in the past, but it is certainly costing us no additional money or rights at this time. In that connection, if we had not been engaged in conservation and propagation on the west coast we would not have had this basis for asking the Japanese to waive any rights. That is the only cost. There is no new cost. All three countries are firmly convinced that the conservation of the fisheries on the high seas is a necessity, and that more and more the nations of the world will come to depend on the sea for more of their food. This agreement will allow the maximum of exploitation and at the same time a sustained yield of fish.
It is not my intention and I do not think it is the intention of the government to press for early ratification of the agreement for two reasons. First, the majority of the governments that signed the Japanese peace treaty in San Francisco will have to ratify the peace treaty before anything further can be done. I think hon. members will realize that at the present time Japan is not in a position to sign this agreement, until the peace treaty has been ratified. When this has been accomplished we will then consider when we should ask for the ratification of the fisheries agreement. Second, we want all interested parties to have an opportunity of making representations to us.
We have a standing committee on fisheries, and I would hope that some time during this session they will be called together to consider this agreement. Now that I have made this statement in the house, where I think it is proper that I should do so, I am free to meet with other groups, particularly in British Columbia, to discuss this matter. I have tried to give to the house in as simple and as clear a way as possible not the whole treaty but the results of our meeting. The legal and technical details can be discussed in the committee on marine and fisheries, and if members are interested they can be further discussed in the house when we are asking to have the treaty ratified.
I have already given you the names of the Canadian delegation attending the conference in Tokyo. May I now extend to them my sin-cerest thanks. They worked hard throughout

the whole conference and with good effect. Canada has received the maximum protection without injuring the welfare of any other country, and has obtained something that we did not have before, security for the principal fisheries of British Columbia. I think the members of the delegation are entitled to our sincere thanks.
I wish also to add to the names mentioned that of Mr. Arthur Menzies, head of the Canadian legation in Tokyo, our host, our guide, our friend and counsellor. This includes of course Mrs. Menzies. Ladies are always called upon on occasions of this kind to depart from their normal routine, if in such positions there ever is a normal routine. We were much impressed by the good work that is being carried out in Tokyo for all of Canada and particularly for the boys who are in the forces in Korea and who visit Tokyo from time to time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the statement which has just been read by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew). I am sure that members of the house and the people of British Columbia will appreciate the fact that the minister has taken an early opportunity in the present session to explain this difficult, very complicated and decidedly controversial agreement. Many interests in British Columbia have had doubts as to the soundness of the agreement, and, as the minister himself intimated, the agreement has been questioned and objections to it have been raised. As the minister has suggested, that may be because the people of British Columbia, and particularly the fishermen, have not been fully conversant with all the details and the background. The minister has taken the trouble today to explain some of that background, and I am sure his remarks will be studied with care and interest even though they may not be accepted immediately by people who have another point of view.
I was particularly pleased to hear the minister say that the government was in no hurry to seek ratification of the agreement, and to hear him promise to refer it for the consideration of the standing committee on marine and fisheries. My hope is that every opportunity will be given to call before the committee the parties who are particularly interested in this matter.
It is not my intention this afternoon to say any more about this question. I was asked last fall if I would attend the sixth session of the general assembly of the United Nations as a parliamentary observer. While I was in Paris a further invitation came asking me
The Address-Mr. Pearkes if I would also attend the consultative assembly of the council of Europe which was meeting in Strasbourg. I want to take this opportunity to thank you, Mr. Speaker, through whom the invitation was issued, and the house for granting me the great privilege and remarkable opportunity of attending the meetings of the council of Europe. In the time at my disposal I should like to report to you and the house my impressions of the assembly and to give very briefly the background of the work which the council of Europe is endeavouring to carry out. I do so because I was the only member of this house who was privileged to attend the meetings of the council, and in fact the only member who has ever been there as an official observer. I found my experiences to be both unique and of the greatest value. I would like to pass on in a factual way, certainly not in a controversial manner, the impressions I received from my attendance at those meetings.
It may be of general interest to know that shortly after the cessation of hostilities in world war II Mr. Winston Churchill, while speaking at Zurich, called for the establishment of a European system to ensure a greater degree of unity amongst the nations of that continent. That appeal led to what became known as the European movement, and through that movement the council of Europe was created.
The council of Europe is quite unique. It is different from the assembly of United Nations, and its organization is different from that of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It consists of a consultative assembly and a committee of ministers. The consultative assembly meets annually at Strasbourg in Alsace, a province of France. I would like to digress for a moment to give a word picture of that ancient city of Strasbourg, because I believe it has some bearing upon the results of the consultations of that assembly.
Strasbourg is a very ancient city. The day we arrived there by train it was celebrating its liberation from the Germans after the second world war. Strasbourg has been captured and liberated many times in its long history. When we went to our hotel we looked over blocks of dwellings the roofs of which were almost identical with those depicted in some of the old fairy tale books, such as Hans Andersen. They had very high gables and red slates, with very uneven ridge lines. In the gables were small apertures or windows, seldom having glass in them. Looking over a long vista of these roofs we saw behind them, and towering high above

The Address-Mr. Pearkes them, the century-old cathedral built on a mount which had been a place of worship long before the birth of Christ. That city is also surrounded by very slow moving canals. One saw barges moving up and down those canals in very much the same way they had been moving for many years past. But those barges eventually reached the ocean, and I think they are symbolic of the slow movement toward an objective which is being shown by the council of Europe. That whole city is steeped in history and tradition, and it is on that tradition and history that Europe is slowly advancing and building upon what has gone before.
As I said, the consultative assembly met in Strasbourg. This assembly is composed entirely of national delegations from the fifteen member countries of the council of Europe. There again it is interesting to note that the member countries are not all members of the United Nations, nor are they all members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. All the delegates are elected representatives of the parliaments of their particular countries. That again, I think, is significant, because they were people who had to take a practical view of conditions. They could not be too idealistic, or too far in advance of public opinion in the districts they represent. They represented not only the governments of their countries but also the opposition parties, so an observer from Canada had an opportunity to talk with representatives of all parties who were there.
In the assembly the delegates are seated alphabetically. You might find a delegate from France sitting next to a delegate from Greece, simply because of the initials of their surnames. Each delegate votes individually, not by countries, so you avoid the bloc system of voting which is quite noticeable at the United Nations. The resolutions and recommendations adopted by the assembly are then passed on to the committee of ministers, whence, if approved, they are referred to the governments of the various countries.
As I said in the beginning, the object of the council is to ensure greater unity amongst the countries of Europe. At the first session of the consultative assembly, which was held three or four years ago, it was shown that there was no hope of securing a federation of the whole of Europe at that time, so an alternative proposal was advanced which has become known as the functional approach. By that is meant the setting up of specialized authorities designed to ensure European cooperation in specific fields such as agriculture, defence, transportation and trade relationships, where a definite problem might

be dealt with. But the ultimate responsibility of accepting or rejecting it would rest with the national government. On the other hand the federalists, represented very largely by French and Italian delegates, adhere to the theory of supranational authorities responsible to some international parliamentary body. As the debates went on it appeared that the functional approach seemed for the time being the most practical way of bringing about greater unity among the various countries.
The first specialized authority to be proposed was the Schuman plan in connection with coal and steel, which was advanced in 1950. At the same session Mr. Winston Churchill moved a resolution in the consultative assembly calling for a European army, which subsequently was developed into the Pleven plan which no doubt we shall be discussing some time later in this house. When Mr. Churchill advanced his proposal he was anxious to attract western Germany to the western cause, and he used these words:
There is no revival of Europe, no safety of freedom for any of us, except in standing together, united and unflinching.
I ask this assembly-
That was the consultative assembly of the council of Europe.
-to assure our German friends that if they throw in their lot with us, we shall hold their safety and freedom as sacred as our own.
Statements had been made shortly before that, and have since been repeated by Herr Grotewohl, leader of the German party in east Germany, which had attracted a great deal of attention. He referred to the neutralization of Germany, and by that he was suggesting that a vacuum might be created in Germany where there would be no armed forces. The occupational forces of Russia, France, the United Kingdom and the United States would be withdrawn, and there would be a neutralized zone. At this time it was felt, and I believe it was felt by a majority of the people attending the council of Europe, that such a program would be tantamount to placing the whole of Germany at the disposal of the U S.S.R., and that it would be handing over that vast territory to the communists.
The integration of western Germany, therefore, within the European community was considered of paramount importance. It was only by permitting western Germany into the council of Europe on a basis of equality that the German people could be given the necessary prestige and authority. As you know, the Labour government, which was then in

Great Britain, did not take part in the discussions on either the Schuman or the Pleven plan. In due course the Schuman plan was adopted and the treaty signed, while plans for the European army had progressed. The position taken by the British delegates at the consultative assembly this year was that of close association with, but not unconditional participation in, either the Schuman plan or the European army plan.
I believe the position of the British delegates was summed up quite well by Lady Tweedsmuir, who was one of the British delegates and who spoke extremely well. She used these words:
We believe that our conception of a working partnership in Europe is right, not only because we face adversity now, but that it is right forever. We put our trust not so much in treaties, because history has shown that these can be broken. What really matters is whether Britain will share with all her friends both good days and bad in the time to come, and I can say that we shall be there.
As I said, there was some disappointment that the British were not prepared to accept unconditionally the proposals of a European army or of the federation of Europe. Mr. Paul Reynaud spoke and said he was profoundly disappointed that the United Kingdom would only associate herself with this movement. The result of this disappointment so openly expressed tended towards a revival of the idea of a limited continental federation which would be limited to those European countries which were anxious and willing to federate. The trend towards this limited federation was encouraged by the attitude of the United States of America.
The United States of America had, as you know, backed the Schuman plan from the beginning, and had given much support to the Pleven plan. Furthermore, this summer a number of congressmen had visited a committee of the council of Europe at Strasbourg, and had come out very strongly for European federation. I refer you to the description I gave earlier of Strasbourg. There were these slowly moving canals. We on this continent come from a land where there are turbulent mountain streams. However, over the centuries those slow moving canals have delivered their barges, shall we say, on the ocean of achievement. The idea of the United States congressmen for immediate federation of Europe represented, I believe, the hurry and rush of a mountain torrent trying to reach the sea. As you know, mountain torrents splash up some water on their banks before they reach their goal.
However, the debates that followed in the assembly made it quite clear that the group of representatives from those Scandinavian countries, Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Iceland, were not prepared to accept any
The Address-Mr. Pearkes closer ties with continental Europe than those which the United Kingdom was prepared to accept. Furthermore, the Benelux countries, Belgium, Netherlands and Luxembourg, also found it difficult to accept federation unless the United Kingdom was a full partner and thus able to provide a counterpoise to what might eventually become a French-German struggle. This impasse emphasized the necessity for the consultative assembly to make a new effort this year to try to find a practical, even if partial, solution which would enable the council to gain some ground in the direction of its ultimate goal. Those are the words which were used in a report from the political committee. The goal, namely of building that unity of Europe, was the raison d'etre of the council.
There was a feeling frequently expressed that, while the desirability of the closest association with the United States was quite self-evident, yet Europe would become more a partner and better able to negotiate with the United States on an equal footing if the countries of Europe were more united. I am not suggesting that there is not gratitude from the countries of Europe for the vast amount of aid which has been given to those countries by the United States. I am suggesting that those countries are anxious to have a say in how that aid will be distributed amongst them. They feel that if they were a united group, then they would be able to negotiate better with the United States. For this reason urgent appeals were made to the United Kingdom once again to participate not only in the European army but in the continental community.
I also heard Mr. Paul Reynaud declare that without Britain the European army plan could not pass the national assembly in Paris. These anxieties which were expressed at the end of last year have to some extent been smoothed over, and the government of the United Kingdom has promised close co-operation with the continental defence community, if and when it comes into being. Mr. Eden has made it quite clear that Britain cannot join a European federation. Therefore, it remains to be seen whether some practical alternative to a limited continental federation can be found. From all that I heard at Strasbourg, I suggest that the crux of the problem is to keep Germany on our side without subjecting Europe to German domination. Despite assurances of close association given by the United Kingdom there were in France, in the Benelux countries and elsewhere, widespread feelings that without

The Address-Mr. Pearkes actual British participation Germany would soon become the dominating partner in any purely continental federation.
Many examples were given of the amazing resilience of the German people and of the industrial recovery which has already taken place in western Germany. It was stated that the general production of industries in western Germany today was almost 150 per cent of that of pre-war days. Later I had an opportunity of motoring for some 200 miles down the Rhine valley and through the great industrial area of the Ruhr. There cities which are connected with the coal and steel industry-such as Essen and Dusseldorf and which we knew had been nearly destroyed during the last war-were now giving visible evidence of the way in which the new plants had risen on the very rubble which was all that had been left of the factories of pre-war days. Everywhere one saw tall chimney stacks belching out smoke. All down that high road one saw a great movement of commercial supplies being moved by tractor, drawn by diesel-driven lorries, sometimes with one or two trailers behind them. To give some idea of the financial recovery of Germany I should like to read a paragraph from a report of a survey which was made for the Council of Europe by the organization for European economic co-operation, and dated November, 1951. This is to be found at page 13:
The German position has improved so fast that by the end of May she had repaid the whole of the special credit granted to her by E.P.U.-*
That is the European payment union.
-and by the end of December her cumulative deficit with E.P.U. has been reduced to some $106 million as against the peak of $469 million at the end of February.
That is February, 1951.
Consequently, it has been decided that the special arrangements under which her trade with member countries is now carried on shall cease at the 1st January, 1852, and that she will proceed to a substantial degree of liberalization as from that date.
I think that brief quotation and that brief description of what I saw personally in the Ruhr valley will give some idea of this amazing growth and recovery in western Germany. The one thing which stood out, however, in all the statements made at Strasbourg by representatives of west Germany was the determination of the Germans once again to become a united nation. As hon. members know, they are divided at the present time, with their eastern provinces taken away from them and handed over to Poland, to Czechoslovakia and to Russia, with Russia occupying the central part of Germany between the Oder and the Elbe, with Berlin an island in the centre of that territory, and with the occupational forces of the west in the part


between the Elbe and the Rhine. I heard the leader of the west German republic delegation-his name was Heinrich von Brentano- say that the division of Germany was one of the main causes for the present disturbed conditions in Europe, and presented a constant threat of war. Then he concluded by saying that the unification of Germany is an imperative necessity.
There is no doubt about it that, amongst many people in Europe, there is a fear that Germany may once again, almost inevitably, become the dominating factor in any European federation. It is for that reason that various delegates advanced the idea of some form of commonwealth relationship for western Europe which could possibly include the United Kingdom rather than having the idea of a limited federation.
Events are moving so rapidly in Europe and they have such a profound influence upon the lives of the people of Canada that I feel it is of great importance that we should take every opportunity to keep in touch with those events. The meetings of the consultative assembly, as I have said before, provide for any member of this house who might be sent there a unique opportunity to meet the leading statesmen of many countries of Europe and also the opportunity of feeling the pulse of Europe. I am most grateful for the opportunity which was afforded to me to attend those meetings at Strasbourg last year. I would strongly recommend that Canada accept, in future, any invitation which may be sent to her to send observers to meetings of this assembly. I know of no better way of ensuring harmony between this country and the countries of Europe than to interest ourselves in their problems. The council of Europe provides the fundamental framework for political and economic co-operation. When these invitations are extended in future, I hope it will be possible for observers from all parties in this house to accept them.
