These are problems which have arisen because of the severe storm damage which took place in that province in the months of December, January and February. It was just prior to Christmas that I first brought to the attention of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) the severe losses that had been suffered by the lobster men, and I asked

that some investigation be made as to the damage that had been done. When we came back for those few days between Christmas and New Year's I again asked a question, and I asked how much had been done towards starting this survey. He told me then that it was being investigated, and it would be some time before they had a report. I know that during the month of January the local fisheries officers and the economist from the department district office of Halifax were in the counties of Digby, Yarmouth, Shelburne, Queens, Lunenburg and part of Halifax, the counties which suffered very heavily, to make a careful survey of the losses. I have on various occasions interviewed officials of the department and the minister concerned, and written them concerning this matter, and I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the time has now come when it must be said on the floor of this house so that the people at large may have some idea of the immensity of the losses suffered by these hard-working independent fishermen of Nova Scotia.
We find that in those five and a half counties of Digby, Yarmouth, Shelburne, Queens, Lunenburg and part of Halifax-these counties compose the lobster district, generally known as district No. 4-the loss in damage and ruin of lobster traps alone amounted to some $750,000. The loss of $750,000 by individual fishermen of five and a half counties is a severe loss. I do not believe very many people have any idea of the work or the cost of building a lobster trap. For the benefit of those who do not come from fishing constituencies I am going to outline just briefly what a lobster trap consists of and why it costs as much as it does.
The ordinary lobster trap which is used in our waters is approximately four feet long and is composed of laths. Many of them are four bowed traps in the construction of which are used nails, sills, shoes, bows, twine, oil and paint, three nozzle rings. They also use marline, spindles, bait bags, ballast, swivels, staples, half-way buoys, and buoys on the top of the water. Then there is a galvanized ring and a twenty-five fathom mooring. The cost is approximately $7. I say that, Mr. Speaker, realizing that that does not take into consideration the cost of the labour involved.
These fishermen are financed or outfitted by the dealers in the area in a great many instances. The situation has arisen this last fall, during December and during the months of January and February, that the losses are such that many of these dealers cannot advance any further credit to the fishermen concerned. Therefore the time has now come when the fishermen in the area cannot get financial assistance, and a good many

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for the dinner recess I had just finished attempting to explain something of the severity of the losses which have been suffered by the fishermen in Nova Scotia. I mentioned that the loss in lobster traps alone amounted to three quarters of a million dollars. Perhaps many hon. members have no realization of what that loss means. It is not just in terms of dollars. I had referred to the material that goes into lobster traps, to the value of $6 to $7 apiece. When 125,000 traps are lost that represents a loss of three quarters of a million dollars. In order to give you an idea of the actual material involved, if those four-foot traps were placed end to end you would have them strung for one hundred miles along the coast.
This loss is of great concern to the fishermen because it represents their means of livelihood. I maintain that their loss is so great that it cannot be overcome without some assistance. I mentioned also the damage to government-owned structures and I should like now to refer briefly to the damage to privately-owned structures in Digby-Yarmouth. I have received innumerable letters, telegrams and petitions outlining the problems which have been created by this disaster and pleading for assistance. I should like to read three paragraphs in one of these petitions, as follows:
We, the undersigned, fishermen, fish processors and fish buyers of East Ferry, Digby county, Nova Scotia, do hereby petition both the federal Department of Fisheries and the Department of Trade and Industry of the province of Nova Scotia for assistance to help in the rehabilitation of the fishing industry of East Ferry which was totally destroyed in the disastrous storm which swept this coast on February 27, 1952.
Appended below will be found a list of the above mentioned fishermen, fish processors and fish buyers together with statements of the loss suffered by each of them. This loss has resulted in the total destruction of the fishing industry of East Ferry and has created a situation whereby assistance must be forthcoming from some governmental agency if the industry is to be rehabilitated and the people of the community of East Ferry prevented from undergoing severe hardship
We urge your prompt and favourable consideration of our petition. Our case is desperate and assistance is urgently needed.

The village of East Ferry suffered the greatest loss, but the villages of Tiverton, Freeport and Westport also suffered considerable loss. In the village of East Ferry the fishing plants, the equipment, the stock in the plants, the wharves upon which the plants were erected

everything was damaged and washed out to sea. The result is that that area has practically no means of making a living. I should like to read in part a letter which I received from one man who is very much concerned:
This community of East Ferry, Digby county, suffered a very severe blow during the gale of February 27 and 28, when in the screaming blizzard which took place at that date, nearly all the fish processing plants, fish houses, freezer plant, lobster car, traps, boats and gear were swept away or smashed into kindling wood and torn metal and debris.
These plants and1 equipment represent the work of a great many people of this community over the past twenty years and under the circumstances as exist today, and through their own efforts at this time, are to all intents and purposes practically irreplaceable. These men who have undergone this severe loss simply have not got the dollars to rebuild and replace.	.
All these letters set out the facts. They are all of the same tenor. They are all written in the finest tone and in the most courteous language. They all plead for assistance. I mentioned plants, wharves, equipment in the plants, but in addition these men have lost their boats. In that same storm on February 27 and 28 one 60-foot dragger was lost as well as several 40-foot boats. Dozens of boats were severely damaged, some of them beyond repair. At least ten lives were lost. My sympathies go out to the families of those who met this terrible fate, and particularly to a lady in one village in Shelburne county who lost her father, her husband and two brothers.
I have talked with fishermen in the area and to those who are interested in the fishing industry. That is our basic industry, it is an industry that affects practically everyone. I find it hard to explain to these people that we are able to provide assistance for other areas, for other communities, for other basic industries, but find it difficult to provide assistance for this industry. I am not going to go into the details, but I have been asked by these people to explain how it is that in the case of the fire at Cabano an amount of $300,000 was provided. It is true that that was provided 50 per cent by this government and 50 per cent by the Quebec government. Then $2,500,000 was provided in the case of the Rimouski fire by the federal government, with an additional $330,000 for the Rimouski schools. Assistance was granted in the case of the Fraser river and Red river floods. I do not know just how many millions it has taken to repair dikes and other damage. Not

for one moment do I object to any of these expenditures, and neither do the people in my constituency; but they do find it hard to understand why assistance is given to these other areas when it seems so difficult to engender any sympathy for their plight or to obtain the assistance which I contend is so urgently needed.
It might well be that we should have something similar to the P.F.A.A. whereby a certain percentage of the value of the catch would be placed in a special fund to provide for these cases, just as is done in the case of crop damage or crop loss in the west. Only last week we were able to change the order of business in this house and spend three days debating the severe outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. I have not one objection to that; but I do submit, and I hope during the course of this debate other hon. members from the maritimes who are familiar with this problem will support me, that in view of the severity of this problem some assistance should be given.
As far as Nova Scotia is concerned there is what you might call a short-term problem as well as the long-term problem. The longterm problem I suggest can be met by some form of insurance. The short-term problem is the one that at the present worries most of our people. Fishermen do not have unemployment insurance nor do they come under workmen's compensation. During the thirties when other areas were receiving direct assistance or relief the fishermen of Nova Scotia received nothing from the federal government or any other government. They struggled through because they are hardy and independent. Now they have suffered a loss which I feel makes them entitled to some assistance.
We had a somewhat similar situation in 1938 when very severe losses occurred. At that time the federal government made loans to the provincial fishermen's loan boards, which in turn made loans to the fishermen. Therefore they were able to have the necessary funds to repair their damaged boats, to replace boats that were lost and to replace gear which had been damaged or lost. Mr. Speaker, throughout this debate speeches have been made on a great many subjects. I hardly think there is anything in the speech from the throne which has not been dwelt on at some length during the debate. Nevertheless, in looking over the speech from the throne one of the things that attracted my attention was something mentioned in the very first part o. the speech namely, inflation. That is one of the matters about which I wish to speak for a few moments. It seemed to occupy the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) probably more than anything else. The speech from the throne refers to inflation in this way:
Inflationary pressures are still being strongly felt and require the maintenance of anti-inflationary measures.
One of the things which the government has recognized at the very beginning of the session, one of the things first mentioned in the speech from the throne, is the continuance of the government's anti-inflationary measures. I think I hardly need remind the house and the people of Canada that the anti-inflationary measures presented to the house in the last budget were not as effective as was expected by the people of Canada and were not as successful as was expected by the government. In speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the Prime Minister had this to say, as recorded at page 171 of Hansard for March 6:
May I say that we have been endeavouring to deal with the high cost of living, particularly since the outbreak of the Korean war which, as the hon. gentleman has said, put a pressure upon prices, not only in this country but in all the free nations of the world, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that in the methods that we have adopted to combat that inflation we have been as fortunate-I will perhaps not say as wise-as any others anywhere in the world, although we have not been able to do as is suggested, namely, devise anti-inflationary measures that would be sufficient to outbalance the inflationary pressures. What has happened here is what has happened everywhere else in the world. Again I am not boasting.
Then he goes on to say:
For the last couple of months there has not been anything startling in the cost of living index issued by the bureau of statistics, but there appears to be a trend that indicates a stabilization.
I want to refer again to one sentence of what he said and remind the house of it. He said:
. . . we have not been able to . . . devise antiinflationary measures that would be sufficient to outbalance the inflationary pressures.
I am not surprised that we find that the cost of living index has practically remained stationary since it reached an all-time high. In fact the only change in the cost of living

index has been a fraction of one point, seven-tenths of a point. The Prime Minister points to that with some pride and satisfaction, and says it is an indication that at last we have achieved some measure of stabilization. But when he frankly admits that the government has no device or method which will offset this inflationary trend, at least I think we can say in his favour that he has been frank enough to admit that the government has not found a solution to the problem.
Of course the Prime Minister referred to the other countries of the world and says those other countries have been affected just as we have. That is not the case, however. In the United States there has been a greater reduction in price levels than we have seen, and when you compare the wages paid in the United States with the wages in Canada you find a great difference. When you look at the standard of living of the people of the United States and compare it with the standard of living of our people there is also a great difference.
There are at least some in Canada who realize that this drop of -7 in the cost of living index is not an indication of a downward trend, and that it does not mean the situation is stabilized. Under the heading "Nice if it lasts" the Ottawa Citizen of Thursday, March 6, had this to say:
It is cheering news for Canadians that the monthly official cost of living index figure has dropped by seven-tenths of a point, the second time in three months that the index has varied its monotonous upward march. The fall is from a record mark of 191-5 to a figure as at February 1 of 190-8.
Many people, however, will restrain their jubilation. They have been caught before. Several times during the past few years the course of inflation appeared1 to be arrested, with the appearance of a fractional drop in the cost of living index, but presently it was on its merry way again. It may also be that the decline of seven-tenths of a point is the biggest decrease in the index in nine years. Encouraging though it is, however, this figure of minus 0-7 does not look quite so impressive alongside the monthly record for the year 1951. Until December, the changes were all plus: 2-7 points, 4-5, 2-1, 0-2, 2-1, 3-5, 1-3, 0-9, 0-6, 0-8 and finally minus 0-1. In January the index moved up again, the change being 0-4 points. It will be time to rejoice when the official index shows a constant downward curve for several successive months, and with the changes expressed in more than fractions of a single point.
I think that is probably the correct view; and while the Prime Minister seems quite jubilant over the fact that there was a drop of -7 in the official index, that is no assurance that we are beginning a downward trend.
The measures adopted by the government in the last budget brought down in this house are quite well known to the people of Canada. In the first place the sales tax was increased by 25 per cent. By that 55704-21J
The Address-Mr. Johnston means the government hoped to drain off any surplus purchasing power in the hands of the people and halt the pressure that was causing prices to rise. That did not happen; as a matter of fact the result was exactly the opposite. Then they increased the excise tax from 15 per cent to 25 per cent. Then, not satisfied with that, thinking the standard of living of the people was still too high, they imposed a surtax of 20 per cent. These were tremendous increases in taxation, particularly when the people were already faced with overwhelming bills every time they had to pay their income tax. That might not have been so bad if it had produced the desired effect, but it did not. The evidence is quite clear that even while those measures were being put into effect the cost of living continued to rise.
In a radio broadcast to which I listened some two or three months ago, the Prime Minister appealed to the people of Canada to increase production, saying that was the thing which would cause a lowering of prices. Well, strange as it may seem, that is exactly what the people of Canada did. Speaking from memory I believe there was an increase of something like 16 per cent in the over-all production of manufactured articles in this country. When we look around we see evidence of that fact. In every store we find goods that could not be sold. Washing machines and refrigerators were piling up in the stores; so were automobiles, to such an extent that the automobile industry bad to lay off workers. Yet the -cost of living continued to rise. Businessmen were not able to sell the goods they were producing, so we had a surplus of goods and a deficiency of purchasing power. If the program brought in by the government -at that time had been effective surely we would have seen a drastic drop in prices, but such was not the case. Throughout the year prices continued to rise, and now we have a drop of seven-tenths of one point. Surely that is indicative of the lack of success of the measures applied by the government in an attempt to halt inflation. The Prime Minister acknowledges that fact when he says, "We have not been able to devise anti-inflationary measures that would outbalance the inflationary pressures." Surely when the next budget comes down we may expect the government to have devised some effective anti-inflationary measures. If they have not, this country will have something to really complain about.
I am not at all surprised, though, that the government's program did not offset the increase in living costs. Not only did they increase the sales tax and excise tax and impose a surtax; they put on credit restrictions so people would not be able to buy the

The Address-Mr. Johnston goods which were being produced. The Prime Minister appealed tor production. He got production. But at the same time he made it impossible for the people of Canada to buy the goods that were being produced, and thereby created surpluses of all goods.
These measures taken by the government were not only sufficient to meet the requirements as far as revenue was concerned; as has been indicated on other occasions there is a grand surplus of nearly $722 million. If the government sincerely believed that would offset the increase in the cost of living then it might have been worth while, but the fact is that it did not; and of course the people suffered. The government says the people who have this money-and mind you it struck the poor harder than anyone else-really do not know how to take care of their own purchasing power, so the government took it away from them by way of taxes, I suppose in the belief that they knew better how to deal with it than the people who had earned it. So this tremendous surplus of $722 million was piled up. Then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) says we are going to use some of that to reduce the national debt. When I listened to that statement the other day it made me laugh. The federal government has no intention of materially reducing the national debt. A few years ago the governor of the Bank of Canada made a reference to that in the banking and commerce committee. He said that any nation that would do away with its national debt would be foolish. Without a national debt no nation is prosperous, and the governor of the bank referred to Africa as an example. He is the outstanding financial spokesman who backs up the government's program.
I often thought that if the Minister of Finance were serious in his desire to reduce the national debt he would have introduced a piece of legislation which would have laid plans for effectively reducing and eliminating the national debt. We now pay in taxes close to a half billion dollars every year for interest charges on that national debt. If the debt were eliminated I think that would be an effective way of saving the people that amount in taxes every year. I know some hon. members will refer to the fact that this debt is owned by the people of Canada. That is a lot of rubbish, because by far the great majority of the people in Canada do not own these bonds today and have no share in the national debt. Some people may own $100 or $200 worth of bonds, and there may be the odd one with $500, but very few have more than that. If the government were sincere about eliminating the national debt to save

this country a half a billion dollars every year, they could very well take Alberta as a pattern.
In 1935 the little province of Alberta, because it was a small province then, paid 51 cents out of every dollar of taxation in interest charges. They have reduced that to the point where they now pay 7 cents out of every dollar, and legislative provision has been made whereby in the matter of twenty-two or twenty-three years that provincial debt will be wiped out. The people of that province will be saved half their taxes, and that money can be used, as some of it is now, for social services and other benefits. If this government were really interested in reducing the national debt they would introduce legislation which would make that promise effective. But of course they do not mean any such thing.
I want to refer to this inflationary measure from another point of view. Of course, what I say probably will not have any effect upon the members of this house, but I should like to read an article which was published in the Calgary Albertan of Saturday, September 8, 1951. It is a good Liberal paper, by the way. The Albertan is a Liberal paper, and the Calgary Herald is a Conservative paper. Premier Manning was speaking, and I think he is recognized throughout Canada as being one of the experts when it comes to discussing matters of economics. He has demonstrated that beyond any doubt. In the address which was reproduced in this article Mr. Manning was speaking during the Calgary West by-election. He touched upon this question of inflation and rising costs, and had this to say:
Premier Manning attacked the Liberal propaganda barrage saying "the wise men from the east were most anxious to let it be known that the people of Alberta were not responsible for their prosperity but owed it to the benevolence of the Liberal government in Ottawa." He added that the barrage took credit for social welfare and carefully evaded the question of whether the government was doing anything about the No. 1 problem-the cost of living.
Then, down further he goes on:
After charging the government with doing nothing to keep down the rising cost of living, he said, "I have no hesitation in saying the problem can't be solved under the existing financial set-up."
When you realize, Mr. Speaker, that the present financial system is one which demands debt for its very existence, then you cannot expect any other result than the one the Liberal government achieved in their anti-inflationary measure brought down in the last budget. You cannot expect any more beneficial results from the legislation they will bring down in their next budget; make

no mistake about it. This is one of those systems which always run into a depression or period of inflation, followed then by another period of depression. Throughout our history the only way we have ever gotten out of that mess was by war or preparation for war. Incidentally, it is only preparation for war which gives us this little period of false prosperity now.
But lest some people think that Social Crediters are the only ones that take this view, let me read a short editorial. On many occasions since 1935 when I, along with most of the Social Crediters here, first came to Ottawa, there have been many occasions when members of this party, particularly' the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and the leader of this party, the member for Peace River (Mr. Low), have put forward in clear and unmistakable terms those devices which would have solved our inflation had the government seen fit to carry them out. Not only are Social Crediters interested in this principle, but others are as well. I want to read an editorial from the Western Producer. Probably that paper is one of the most widely circulated of any weekly paper in Canada, certainly in the west. This editorial on inflation reads:
Inflation is a visible symptom of the sickness of our economy. It is evidence, which everyone can see, of the breakdown of finance. The decay has been developing for a long time practically unnoticed except by the acute observer. But under pressure of the present critical period the money system is cracking under the strain and it is quite possible that it may crash completely with consequences for society and the individual impossible to foresee.
Last week a prominent American economist stated publicly that in a decade or so the United States dollar may be worth only five cents in terms of present-day values. We are not among those who accept the word of an economist as the word of God. Some of them have said very foolish things in the past and are capable of being just as foolish again. Nevertheless, allowing full scope for exaggeration and error, the forecast of a five-cent dollar by a responsible professional man cannot be disregarded.
If an individual-any individual-were convinced that he was about to be robbed he would certainly be on the alert and would take every possible precaution to prevent the theft and bring the thief to book. There would be no need to rouse his interest in a matter of such personal concern to him. Yet inflation is just such a thief, more insidious and subtle, but every bit as effective. Unless the rank and file of ordinary people become fully conscious of the threat which hangs over them, unless they come to recognize inflation for what it is, they will almost certainly pay a heavy penalty for their ignorance or complacency.
Now, that is someone who is not classified as a Social Crediter; it is the opinion of someone who has followed economics very closely.
Following that up, Mr. Speaker, I should like to have the permission of the house to
The Address-Mr. Johnston put on Hansard two very short tables. The first one consists of ten lines and the second consists of five. They are tables which tell the story of a $75 savings bond bought in the United States in 1940. The value of the dollar at the time of purchase is taken at par. The first column in this table shows the cash value of the bond which it will be seen increases each year, and the last column shows the actual purchasing power of the cash value which decreased most rapidly. The next table, Mr. Speaker-and these figures are all based on the Bank of Canada statistics-will show plainly that the steady rise in the cash income of workers and others in Canada was merely a mirage. The real income has declined consistently as inflation robbed the dollar of its purchasing power. They are short tables, Mr. Speaker. May I have permission to have them printed in Hansard?

I am referring to the table prepared from United States government statistics and in which reference is made to a United States bond. It was bought in 1940 for $75 and kept until 1950 when it was cashed for $100. The Address-Mr. Johnston
We well recall, Mr. Speaker, that during the war the same picture was painted in Canada. The same appeals were made to the people of Canada. I recall quite well when those campaigns were being carried on. People were told then to save their money to buy a government bond. They were told: If you buy a government bond, in ten years you will be able to buy that fur coat for your wife. They were told: Put your money in government bonds, a gilt-edged security, and you will be able to buy that new car in ten years. People took the government at its word and they bought the bonds. They even went into debt to buy them. The government knew quite well at that time that a great many people who bought those bonds would not be able to hold them for over a week or a month, because provision was made, right at the very outset, for the chartered banks to take these bonds back again. I recall quite well a man coming to my house to sell me a bond on one occasion. When I told him I did not have any money he said: You do not have to have any money; go down to the bank and they will lend it to you. What happened? When people who honestly and sincerely believed what the government told them about the gilt-edged security invested their money in those bonds they found, to their sorrow, that in ten years they had just lost money. They found that they had lost about one-third rather than gained a third. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it was only about two or three weeks ago that the city of North Bay published a letter'-and a copy of this letter was sent to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)-in which they claimed that they had bought $100,000, I think it was, worth of bonds and that when they came to sell them they lost $5 on every $100. They had lost over $5,000 by taking the government at its word. The extraordinary statement made by that city was that they were giving the Minister of Finance their promise on that occasion that they would never buy another government bond and, furthermore, that they would never advocate any other person's buying them either. That is quite a condemnation and it is something which the government should take into consideration.
I do not want to spend any more time on that matter other than to say that if the government persist in trying to bolster up this old, outworn financial system, and if they continue to bring in the type of legislation which they have in the past brought in, they will not be any more successful in combating inflation. Then the Prime Minis-

ter's words again will be only too true, when he says, as reported at page 171 of Hansard:
. . . we have not been able to . . . devise antiinflationary measures that would be sufficient to outbalance the inflationary pressures.
I want to say a word or two about the foot-and-mouth disease. I expect that the government has done everything it can to combat this disease. In fact, I will go so far as to say in this case they have probably been as successful as any others would be under the circumstances. They have now brought down legislation which will be an improvement on that which was contained in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act previously, and by which they are going to give fair and reasonable compensation to those who suffer loss; that is, to those who suffer direct loss. But I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the compensation which the government will give will not reasonably compensate those people for the losses which they suffered. For instance, if a man has a beef herd and those cattle or some of them are ready to market, it may be fair treatment to give him their economic value plus $100 or whatever is fair and reasonable along that line. But if he has a -purebred milking herd, how are the government going to compensate him adequately by giving him its economic value plus a small cash supplement? It just cannot be done, in my opinion. I think there may be occasions when the people who own these cattle may be satisfied with that sort of an adjustment; but I think that in this legislation there should also be provision whereby a man who suffers a loss may require the government to replace that loss. It seems to me that the government can do that, that by so doing they can compensate him much more fairly than they can by giving him a small cash compensation above its economic value. If a man has a milk cow-that is, a registered milk cow-with a high production, you cannot very well put an economic value on that. But the government could and should, in all fairness, replace that cow for that farmer. The same should be done if he has other purebred cattle. Those cattle can be replaced or those sheep can be replaced. If this were done the farmer would be put in the position where he would be restocked; he would be ready to go back into the market again when the period of quarantine had ended.
Then, too, Mr. Speaker, I think the workers who are being affected by this foot-and-mouth disease-and there are many of them despite what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) had to say today-those men who lose their jobs directly because of this foot-and-mouth

disease, should be compensated in some way. I quite realize that you cannot compensate everybody who may be indirectly affected, but these workers who lost their jobs are not affected indirectly; they are affected directly. Certainly the unemployment insurance which they receive will not be sufficient to carry them for long. This quarantine may last for six months, a year or maybe two years. Those people who are working in the packing plants and who are displaced because of the foot-and-mouth disease should have some adequate consideration in this regard.
I want to speak for a moment about war veterans allowance. War veterans allowance has been $40 a month for single men and $70 for married. But, as I indicated a moment ago, because of the inflationary trend, because of the depreciation in the dollar, which is the direct result of government policy, the government must share some responsibility in the lowering standards of living which these veterans are forced to undergo. The sums of $40 and $70 are definitely not sufficient. I understand there is another $10 for those who are in need, but even that is not sufficient. The government should have some consideration for these people who are suffering as a direct result of government policy. They should at least take into consideration the Legion's request and make it $50 for single men and $100 for married men. Even that amount would not give them a decent standard of living, but it would certainly be some compensation.
There is another class of people who need assistance, and need it badly, namely, the old age pensioners. I know that during the last session we passed an old age pensions bill which extended the old age pension to everyone over seventy without a means test. That was a great step forward. It took the government a long time to take that step. The opposition on this side of the house certainly deserves some credit for putting on the pressure; but $40 a month certainly is not sufficient to give these people a decent standard of living. I just received a resolution from the old age pensions association in Calgary. Miss Ethel Baker is the secretary. They are asking for an increase in the old age pension. They are grateful for the old age pension without the means test-of course they would be. We are all grateful because it was given, but certainly we have not anything to stick our chests out over. We say we have given them $40 a month, but we recognize that that $40 is not any more than $20 used to be. I suggest to the government that if the province of Alberta can increase provincial old age pensioners'
The Address-Mr. Johnston receipts by $10 a month, then this federal government could very easily increase the federal old age pensions by another $10 a month. The province of Alberta has gone a step farther. They are now giving $40 a month pension to widows from 60 to 65. They have also extended the benefits from 65 to 69. If the government of Alberta, which is just a province, and has not the means of getting the money that the federal government has, can extend pensions to people aged 60, then surely this government can do likewise. Not only are they extending the pensions in the province of Alberta, but they are giving medical and health services. The federal government is paying $40 pensions to people 70 and over, and the provincial government are giving those same people health and medical benefits plus an extra $10. Can it be that the federal government is so poor, with a $722 million surplus, that they cannot adequately take care of our aged citizens? These are just a few of the things that I should like to mention.
I should like to have mentioned the pressure groups that the Minister of Finance spoke of the other day. I recall something along that line that happened just a little while ago. I went into one of the chain stores in Calgary where we do our buying when we are in Calgary, the Jenkins groceteria, because it is right near our home. On many occasions I have gone into that store when they did not have Imperial Player's cigarettes. I have asked them why and they have told me that they cannot get them from the manufacturer. They could get only a very small supply of canned Imperial Player's tobacco for exactly the same reason. That bears out exactly what the Minister of Finance was telling us the other day in regard to pressure groups. I hope that the Minister of Finance does not become scared too easily.
I should like to have spoken at greater length on it because I know of many other cases which are exactly the same, but my time will not permit me. I think I shall close my remarks now and bring in any further references that I have regarding these matters when they come up under the estimates.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply. I listened to them both and they did very well. They were an honour to their constituencies.
I should like next to express my views about the proposed redistribution measure that is mentioned in the speech from the throne. While I endorse wholeheartedly the

The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) on this matter of redistribution, I am one of those who believe in the constitution. It is proposed that Saskatchewan will lose five seats and Manitoba two seats under the new measure. Parliament should now take into consideration the matter of a constitutional amendment. If the government so desired, they could assure fair and proper representation to those areas upon the prairies which are now to be depleted because of the population there.
There is a principle in the constitution now recognized in the maritime provinces. Regardless of population, the representation of those provinces shall not fall below a certain level, without in any way interfering with the necessary increase that will fall to other provinces in this dominion by reason of the increase in their population. It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, a dominion-provincial conference should be held to decide on a proper guaranteed basis of representation. Failing this, parliament should make the desired amendment to the constitution. That is very important because, as has been pointed out in previous debates here, the centralization of industry has drawn a great many people from these prairie provinces. Notwithstanding that, the greatest part of the necessary food for consumption in this country and for export is produced in those provinces.
Those areas are large for a member to cover and to properly represent the people. It is a very important matter, and parliament should deal with it along the same lines as those that have been suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre and myself. I am sure that, as he said, there is wide support for this, irrespective of party affiliation, everywhere throughout the country.
I should now like to say something about the loss of markets for our agricultural products, and the plight of Canadian agricultural producers, and I think it is rapidly becoming worse. For six years after world war II the problem of expanding supplies of agricultural products was one of primary importance. In that regard we have made very little progress. I followed closely the reports of those attending the FAO conference held in Rome last November. The need of greater production of food was stressed time and time again at that conference. It was pointed out that in the last fifteen years there had been an increase of 12 per cent in the population of the globe, but no more than a 9 per cent increase in the production of food. Many peoples in the world are greatly underfed. That fact is recognized around the world. Our Minister 
of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated that there had been a falling off in the production of milk, pork and beef in Canada since the end of world war II. He said that he thought there would be no increase in the production of meat unless some assurance could be given to farmers that a market would be found for that increased production.
The minister stated that the position in regard to cereals was somewhat better. I listened to the report of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he spoke to the convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held in Montreal last January. He stressed the need for an expansion in the production of food, but admitted, on the other hand, that there was a serious problem in regard to distribution. He argued that an increase was necessary in order to promote peace in the world. But the Prime Minister did not give any kind of assurance to the farmers of Canada that if they did increase the production of food there would be a market for it.
At this same farm gathering the Minister of Agriculture pointed out that the question of international exchange was a matter for the different countries to settle. He wanted to see larger export markets, but he said that the farmers might as well face the facts as they existed. The government by its policies can cause either a decrease or an increase in production and therefore it is in a position to maintain support prices.
Support prices should be established on a parity basis. The present support prices under hogs, eggs, cheese and other dairy products are not based on parity and are much too low. I have often heard it argued in this house as to just what parity meant. I have here a quotation from a statement made in 1939 which I think applies equally to the present time. This reads:
The speaker was talking where his words would do most good-within full earshot of St. James street. He said:
"In my business I am very much worried about this lack of price parity and what I can do with it. I know, for example, that our biggest single block of customers-the farmers of western Canada [DOT]-are not getting enough for their goods to enable them to buy what other people have to sell, and my company cannot hope to prosper unless this exchange of traffic goes on. If we are to have profit, then the farmer must sell wheat and buy other goods as well. It is difficult for him to do that in any volume at the present level of income which he enjoys.
That leads me to think that, unless the price of what the farmer produces is going to rise very rapidly, the rest of us will have to set our minds very seriously to reducing the price of what he buys."

I admit all that, but the plight of the farmer still lives. I realize that the bureau of statistics indicates the great income the agriculturists of this country are receiving today, but those are gross figures. I should like to see the net income from various farm products worked out. This inflationary period has created difficult circumstances which must be faced by the agricultural producer.
The economic division of the Department of Agriculture pointed out last October that farm production costs will be further increased during 1952. I think that is acknowledged by all people. The costs entering into agricultural production are increasing and will continue to increase during the present year. In the past the Canadian farmer has been asked by the government to make sacrifices totalling many hundreds of millions of dollars in order to subsidize the people of Canada and Great Britain with cheap bread. This matter has been discussed in former debates in this house.
Today these same wheat farmers are subsidizing the consumers of 37 nations besides this country to the extent of 59 cents per bushel under the international wheat agreement. On the day this present session opened the quotation under the international wheat agreement, and this applies to domestic consumption as well, was $1.80J per bushel. Class II wheat to other countries was quoted at S2.39g. You could see the difference between the markets. On that same day the price of eastern wheat, basis Montreal, was $2.56 per bushel. This is an inferior grade of winter soft wheat. Those figures indicate the great disparity that exists.
I believe that the wheat agreement will be renegotiated during the coming year and, if so, I urge the authorities to place in the new agreement an escalator clause to overcome this unfair disparity in the prices of Canadian wheat. The Canadian farmer should not be called upon to subsidize the consumers of Canada, Great Britain and many other nations. I know there are people who will argue that he has been subsidized. I would point out that everything he sells must be sold less freight at the marketing point, while everything he purchases must be purchased plus freight at the purchasing centre.
According to the Sanford Evans bureau of statistics, in the period of the first full year following the termination of world war II, that was during 1946, as a result of embargoes 55704-22
The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross and controls imposed by our Canadian government, the difference between the prevailing United States market price and what the Canadian farmers received for his livestock and coarse grains amounted to $378 million. There was that great loss of revenue in that one year. That will give hon. members some idea of the plight in which the livestock producers may find themselves during the coming twelve months. I do not blame the government directly for the situation that exists, but it does give some idea of what these producers will be up against. They have lost an opportunity to obtain that revenue in a time of declining markets.
The success of the Canadian farmer is dependent upon export markets. On February 28, 1950, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth and the countries of the empire to devise policies to restore our lost markets and thereby to provide jobs for our Canadian people.
Following debate the question was put to a vote but was defeated by the solid vote of government supporters against the vote of the combined opposition parties. Since that time the position with respect to export markets has become much worse. We are now faced with unemployment and breadlines in this nation of ours. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) dealt at some length yesterday with the loss of markets and what the government should be doing to revive markets in the British empire. I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did not agree to the extent that he should have.
From the remarks which were tossed across the floor yesterday at the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), I gathered that a united opinion does not prevail amongst the federal cabinet today on the matter of trying to obtain the overseas markets which are now so greatly desired. We face difficulties as a result of other governments placing embargoes and restrictions against our livestock and meat products because of the foot-and-mouth disease in Canada. I hope that when the standing committee on agriculture is called to investigate the actions of the officials of the health of animals branch, with respect to their handling of the disease and the fact that some three months elapsed from the first outbreak before it was termed foot-and-mouth disease, the terms of reference will be broad enough so that officials of the immigration branch may also be questioned on the possibility of this dreaded disease being brought in by immigrants from Europe.

The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross
I know that a statement was made yesterday by the parliamentary assistant exonerating one Willi Bruntjen, who has been under examination at the Hull laboratory. This news has gone throughout the country and it certainly leaves the impression that he could not possibly have brought the virus or disease to Canada. I may be wrong but I do not believe that the test would prove any such thing. It proved there was no virus to be found on his clothing or his body at this time. On the other hand, if they had found the virus I do not believe that would have proved that he had brought it from Europe or had picked it up on the farm near Regina where he worked and where the first outbreak took place. I think it is rather important that the people should understand that. This chap has stated that where he last worked in Europe the entire herd of cattle had gone down with foot-and-mouth disease. I believe that some forty people from the same area in Europe came to Canada on the same boat, and the information I have received indicates that proper inspection and fumigation of their belongings and so forth did not take place. In my opinion this matter should also be thoroughly investigated when the officials of the health of animals branch are being examined.
Some of the forty people I mentioned took employment at the same time in the province of Manitoba with livestock people there. I am very happy that there has been no outbreak of the dreaded disease there yet. However, I think we all must keep our fingers crossed. Yesterday there was word of three new outbreaks in the quarantined area near Regina, and this after the disease was pronounced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as being entirely under control. I know when the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to this statement last night several ministers and others queried him and called upon him to quote the remarks either from Hansard or some other published statement. I have a number of newspapers here containing a Canadian Press dispatch of an interview obtained from the Minister of Agriculture in Regina when he arrived there last Friday. I have the Ontario Intelligencer of Belleville of Saturday, March 8, the day after the interview, in which there is the following:
Federal officials believe they have the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in southern Saskatchewan stopped, agriculture minister Gardiner said Friday night.
Further down there is the following:
Mr. Gardiner, who flew to Regina Friday, said "We don't think foot-and-mouth disease is going to spread. We think it is absolutely under control."

I do not blame the minister for making that statement if he believed that to be the fact, but I think that the people cannot be warned to too great a degree as to how bad the spread of this dreaded disease may become. In the debate on March 3, as found in the first column on page 69 of Hansard, the minister also said:
... by some means or other there had entered the Burns plant at least one animal, if not more, that had the disease. The information we have is to the effect that the disease had gone out from that plant.
Then he spoke about Wascana creek and so on, and I think this view was substantiated by the parliamentary assistant, if I heard him correctly, in answer to a question today. On page 1 of the Winnipeg Free Press of March 7 there is a report of a statement made by Mr. R. Pearson, manager of the Regina plant of Burns and Company. It reads as follows:
R. Pearson, manager of the Regina plant, Burns and Company, said Thursday, "No evidence whatever has been disclosed that foot-and-mouth disease was first discovered in or spread from the company's Regina plant."
The article goes on to report him at some length. These are very conflicting statements and would lead us to believe that the members of the committee on agriculture will have quite a chore to perform when they sit to hear the officials of the health of animals branch. As I said, I hope the government will also allow us to hear officials of the immigration department. On page 3 of the Winnipeg Free Press of March 7 there is an article with the following:
Mr. Connor, Manitoba livestock commissioner, said his department has tried to get some definite direction from authorities at Ottawa regarding the holding of shows and sales without success. He stated further the disease will not likely spread until after the spring break-up when flies and birds will have a chance to carry any live virus which may still be around in the infected areas.
I think that is very important. There will be a few weeks during and after the break-up which will be a serious time. If we get by that period without a further spread of the disease we shall be exceptionally fortunate. With respect to Mr. Connor's statement, one of the first questions asked the minister at the opening of the session by myself was with respect to the Brandon, Regina, Calgary and other fairs, because the purebred breeders were very much concerned. I was most disappointed with the answer I received from the Minister of Agriculture. He certainly gave no lead and left the inference that it was entirely up to those people.
This situation is very serious. It is the first outbreak we have had in Canada. The loss of the infected herds will be bad enough

but the effect on the livestock industry of this nation, which has been developed to a high degree, will have an impact upon the economy of the whole nation. That is something that is very important. Therefore no stone should be left unturned to find out what we can about the entire outbreak.
I should like to refer for a few minutes to the question of inflation and overtaxation. 1 listened closely to the Minister of Finance last Friday setting up what I rather thought was a smokescreen when he applied the term "lobbyist" to the automobile and tobacco associations, and intimated that they had gone beyond any reasonable bounds. Like every other member of the house, I do not believe in lobbyists who are only out for their own particular interests and are not concerned about the well-being of the nation as a whole. However, I think the automobile industry has a just grievance. I have never been able to understand why there should be such a great difference with respect to the taxes and the ultimate price of an automobile in the United States and in Canada. There is altogether too great a difference and has been for some years. On farms and in many other places an automobile or truck is an essential requirement. I should like to refer to certain figures cited by the Canadian automobile manufacturers research service comparing the price of a Chevrolet sedan in 1939 and in 1951. Excise taxes jumped 7,305 per cent in that period, or from $4.81 to $356.22, while sales taxes increased from $59.70 to $142.49, an increase of 138 per cent dollarwise. Then there were the credit restrictions which made it very difficult for many people to purchase a car at all although they needed one in their daily vocations. I think much of the taxation imposed in the last budget was unjust and unfair. We have had cited in detail the case of the electric iron imported from the United States, where the factory price was $5. When you added the duty, the excise tax, the sales tax and the various mark-ups it brought the retail price to the consumer in this country to $14.86. Many people do not realize just what these sales taxes and mark-ups amount to. They are hidden taxes, and constitute a system of taxation which I deplore and very much dislike.
These increased taxes have added to the cost of production and the cost of living in this country. This increased and unnecessary taxation leading to a surplus of some $721 million has increased the difficulties of a great many Canadian citizens beyond all reason. I am surprised that the Minister of Finance takes the matter so lightly. It is very serious for many people who are finding it extremely difficult to provide for them-55704-22i
The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross selves and their families. I was disappointed the other day to hear the Prime Minister say the people could not expect very much in the way of tax reduction at this time. I believe the economy of this country is getting far out of balance as a result of the taxation system brought in by this government.
Now there is another matter I should like to refer to, and that is the international peace garden; I am happy to see the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) in his seat. This is an area consisting of 2,340 acres, 1,452 acres in Canada donated by the Manitoba government and 888 acres on the United States side donated partly by Washington and partly by the state of North Dakota. This garden is situated in the Turtle mountains, a range of hills rising to some 2,500 feet above sea level and extending 45 miles east and west and 20 miles north and south. They are also located midway along the great undefended 3,987 miles of boundary line between Canada and the United States, and on the boundary of the constituency I have the honour to represent in this house.
The international peace garden is incorporated under the laws of Manitoba and North Dakota, and has been recognized by the governments of both Canada and the United States. Further work on this project should be the responsibility of the federal government, in the first place because the whole proposal is international. The dominion government has already expended considerable money on this area, through the government of Manitoba.
It is interesting to recall a paragraph in the speech from the throne at the opening of the Manitoba legislature on February 29, 1932, at about the time this garden was opened. It stated:
A memorable event of the past year is the provision made for the peace garden in the Turtle mountain region of Manitoba and North Dakota.
This international project ought to have a prominent place in the peace chronicles of the present era, when every thinking person in the world is compelled to realize that one of the most important questions facing our civilization is that of world peace, friendship and co-operation.
An editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune of that date said:
It is a worthy, a splendid project, and one that has the enthusiastic approval not only of the people of Manitoba and western Canada but of other millions in both countries. Some of the most magnificent monuments in the world have been erected to commemorate lost causes, vanished glories and ruined hopes. A peace garden, let us hope, will symbolize in its own living beauty, ever more cordial relations between the two great countries.
On July 24, 1932, the official opening of the garden took place and people were

The Address-Mr. J. A. Ross assembled from great distances in the central west, both Americans and Canadians. Two great world wars and the economic and financial problems arising therefrom, together with possible military requirements in the future, are drawing these nations into continuous and closer collaboration and co-operation. This practical demonstration is proof positive that peace between nations is more than an idle dream. It is an accomplished fact.
Some of the reasons these sites were selected were: First, the natural scenic beauty of the area; second, the wide variety of trees, shrubs and wild flowers found growing there; third, the abundance of wildlife including birds native to the district; fourth, the large number of small lakes located in the Turtle mountains; fifth, the fact that the location is almost the geographical centre of the North American continent; sixth, the fact that it is located on the only hard-surfaced highway running north and south, from northern Manitoba through the United States down to Mexico and into the countries of South America; seventh, the fact that no physical barriers, such as rivers, mountains or gorges, stand in the way of free movement of people across the boundary in the designated area. A plaque has been erected upon which the following appears:
To God in His Glory
We two nations dedicate this garden and pledge ourselves that as long as men shall live we will not take up arms against one another.
The plans contemplate the erection of an international peace tower as a symbol of peace between our two great nations, and a suitable war memorial to the thousands of young men and women who give their lives in the last two world wars in the defence of everything we hold to be dear in life. Associated with this memorial js to be a little chapel where friends of loved ones may seek comfort and consolation. Plans are being made for tourist accommodation, picnic grounds, public assemblies and recreational facilities. Customs and immigration offices are to be erected on the site to facilitate the movement of people across the boundary.
A great deal of public support is already manifest. Women's organizations, churches, service clubs, boards of trade, returned soldier organizations and many similar bodies as well as a large section of the public are showing a desire to help in the promotion of this worthy project. More and more will United States tourists be drawn northward by the magnetic attraction of our national parks; and these tourists spend a great deal of money while travelling. May I emphasize the intriguing fact that instead of being situated

in the far east or in the distant west, this garden is actually located within 30 miles of the exact centre of the North American continent. Surely that is a fitting place for it.
A good deal of money is yet required for the work to be done in this garden. The government of the United States has voted $100,000 for this project as compared to $15,000 annually by the Canadian government. Now the Minister of Resources and Development has stated that no money will be made available for this project during the fiscal year 1952-53. Many organizations such as women's institutes, the I.O.D.E., the Eastern Star, chambers of commerce and so on wholeheartedly support this worth-while project. This was very dear to the late J. E. Matthews of Brandon, because the city of Brandon is only some 60 miles to the north and it meant a good deal to those people. I well remember going with Mr. Matthews to interview the then Minister of Mines and Resources in 1949, I think it was, when the government agreed to put this item in the estimates. I believe the late Mr. Matthews also accompanied a delegation to Washington when the government of the United States decided to make its appropriation. I have a resolution which is typical of many I have received from different organizations. This comes from the horticultural society of Manitoba and reads:
Whereas, the international peace garden is a living memorial in a sadly troubled world to the practicability of peace between neighbouring countries; and
Whereas, the governments of both Canada and the United States have given financial support to this project; and
Whereas, it has been publicly announced that, notwithstanding the continued support by the United States government of this project, the government of Canada has decided that no money will be made available for the fiscal year 1952-53, despite the fact that billions have been appropriated for war preparations:
Be it therefore resolved, that this 54th annual convention of the Manitoba horticultural association express our very great disappointment at this decision by the government of Canada, and respectfully request that the matter be reconsidered;
And be it also resolved, that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Prime Minister of Canada, to the Minister of Agriculture for Canada, and to the members of parliament for Manitoba; and that a copy be forwarded also to the minister of agriculture for Manitoba.
Now, I fully realize that members have interviewed the minister during the past year when it was learned that there would not be provision in the estimates this year for this garden. I believe the president of this organization is an able and outstanding man, Mr. D. G. McKenzie, who has been chairman of the Canadian board of grain commissioners and a past minister of agriculture in Manitoba. I believe that, as president of this

organization, he interviewed the minister. As is pointed out in this resolution, the minister has not seen his way clear to providing a grant. I would hope that even during these troubled times, when we are spending such gigantic sums for national defence, the minister would yet reconsider the matter and make provision in the supplementary estimates for a grant for this very worthy project.
I think it is important because the people in Washington will wonder why, if Canada cannot provide anything, they should be expected to vote continued grants. I really believe the amount we have received has been a token grant; it was not a great deal of money. While I know the minister has to pare his expenditures, I hope he will reconsider and give heed to the representations he has had from all of these very worthy organizations and officials. While the estimates are prepared for this year, I hope he will yet see his way clear to providing a sum in the supplementary estimates for this worthy cause.

However, Mr. Speaker, I first wish to express my congratulations to the mover of this motion, the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George), and the seconder, the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier).
The hon. member for Westmorland is a member of this house who has distinguished himself not only in speaking in this chamber but in the work he has done in connection with committees. He certainly has earned for himself the honour of moving this motion, and the manner in which he carried out his responsibility added to his prestige and I am sure was a great satisfaction to his constituents.

He gave us a good description of the Lake St. John district which he represents with such distinction in this house. He did not fail to mention the blueberries of his district which are so well-known everywhere.
While I am speaking in French, I wish to congratulate also the Speaker of this house on the great success he achieved last year
The Address-Mr. Dickey as a student in the French summer courses at Laval university. We English-speaking Canadians are proud to learn that the Speaker of this house devoted a good deal of his holidays to the learning of the French language and we are very glad of the progress he has made.
(Text):
I also wish, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) on the very fine speech that he made in this debate this afternoon. The importance to this nation of the maritime ports is so fundamental that it is most important that the attention of this house be drawn to the need of maintaining and expanding the port facilities in our maritime provinces. I am sure that not for many years have the needs of the port of Saint John been so eloquently or so completely placed before this chamber.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the member for Digby-Yarmouth has, with eloquence and great effect, discussed a matter of serious and immediate concern, not only to him and to his constituents, not only to the members representing the maritime provinces, but to all the members of this house and the country as a whole. Fisheries is one of the basic industries of our national economy. It is important in the martimes. It is important on the Pacific coast, and it is of growing importance in the central part of our country in the great fresh water lakes, and in the salt water of Hudson bay at the north of Ontario and in Manitoba.
However, the fishing industry is of special importance and interest to the maritime provinces because it is such an important part of the livelihood of such a large number of our people. The fishing industry has many difficult problems to meet of a long-range nature, and I am glad to say that much progress is being made in tackling those problems in a scientific and constructive manner. We can all be delighted with the progress that has been achieved. The immediate and present problem relates to the tragic effects which have resulted from a series of very destructive storms which have swept the maritime provinces over the last few months. As a result of these storms, the shore fisheries and the shore fishermen have suffered very grievously. The term "shore fishery" is used to distinguish operations close to the ports and to the shores of the maritime provinces as compared with the deep sea operations on the banks which are farther removed from our coasts.
Generally speaking the people engaged in the shore fisheries use small boats. They use the traditional means of fishing, such as moored nets, trawls, lobster pots and the like. In addition to going down to the sea
334	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Dickey to fish, in a large part they manufacture their own equipment and completely maintain it through their own labour. For the most part these shore fishermen live in small coastal towns and villages. Many of the members of this house will have, through personal knowledge, a realization of the beauty and charm of many of these delightful communities.
I am sure there is not a member in this house who has not seen, through photographs or paintings, some of the charms of those communities that dot the shores of the harbours, coves and bays of our maritime provinces. In good times the life of those living in these fishing villages is as happy and contented as is the life of any Canadians, no matter where they may be found; but the tragic fact is that the economy of these villages is completely dependent on the prosperity of the shore fishing industry. When losses are suffered, such as those which have been suffered over the last few months, the effect is felt not only by those who are actively engaged in the fisheries but by the entire population of those villages, from the eldest citizen to the youngest child; and in many cases it is the children who suffer most.
This succession of storms has been without precedent for many years. The last storm involved the tragic loss of a number of lives of men actively engaged in fishing. This loss of life emphasizes not only the hazards of this occupation but also the exceptional violence of the storms. I am sure that all the members of this house will join in an expression of sincere sympathy to those who have been so sadly bereaved.
In addition to this loss of life, however, crippling loss of equipment has been suffered by many of the fishermen and also-as was pointed out by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth-a loss of wharves and factories by small fish operators. I will not bore the house with figures or any suggestion of the total of this loss of equipment; because even the total figure would not tell the whole story. It is the loss of even the meagre resources of many of these men which creates a situation which, I submit, demands an immediate and effective solution.
The hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth properly drew a parallel between the situation which is facing many of the fishermen in the maritimes at the present time, particularly those in Nova Scotia, with the situation which faced the residents of the Fraser valley when they suffered so grievously from floods, that of the residents of the Red river valley and the city of Winnipeg when they suffered so grievously from
[Mr. DickeyJ

floods, and that of the residents of the town of Rimouski and the town of Cabano when they, in their turn, suffered disastrous fires. He also pointed out the further parallel between the situation of the fishermen and that facing many of our livestock operators and the farmers who get a large portion of their living from the raising of beef and pork by reason of the threat of the plague of hoof-and-mouth disease.
It might be well, Mr. Speaker, just to outline three points which indicate how close this parallel is. Those farmers who have been affected by this hoof-and-mouth disease have lost, through destruction, their property and their very stock in trade. In the second place, they have lost for the time being their means of livelihood. In the third place, they are faced with the problem of rebuilding their livestock herds from the very beginning. Those things are recognized-and properly so, I submit-as requiring for the people who suffered those losses some compensation and some assistance. The fishermen for whom the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth spoke and for whom I am speaking throughout my constituency, throughout the province of Nova Scotia and throughout the maritimes, have also suffered the loss of their property and the loss of their stock in trade. They too have lost, not only in the last week or so but to a large extent over a period of several months, their very means of livelihood; and they too are faced with the necessity of rebuilding their equipment or replacing their nets and their traps and, in many cases, their boats. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that parallel is complete and that this situation, equally with the other, should be recognized as requiring some compensation and some assistance for those who are suffering.
What can be done about this situation? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that so far as the federal authority is concerned we should be ready and willing to co-operate with such provincial and municipal authorities as may be appropriate to work out a reasonable and effective program of immediate compensation. Second, from the federal point of view immediate consideration should be given to a program of public works. Many of the protective works, wharves and facilities which existed in the fishing areas of the maritime provinces have been either damaged or destroyed. Immediate steps should and must be taken to repair and rebuild those structures. This work will have a double value, in replacing needed facilities and also in providing work which will be a measure of direct relief to those who now need it so badly.

I have made these remarks with the express intention of supporting the stand so eloquently expressed by the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth, in order to bring to the attention of this house the actual situation which now exists and to bring it to the attention not only of this house but of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and his colleagues in the cabinet, for the purpose of enlisting their sympathetic interest and their consideration of immediate remedial action.
I should like to conclude, as the hon. member for Digby-Yarmouth concluded, by pointing out that this is not the first time that the fishing industry has suffered grievous difficulties. In common with most other people in Canada, the shore fishermen of the maritime provinces suffered grievously indeed during the years of depression, the years of the hungry thirties. It should be remembered that in those difficult days the fishermen, particularly those of Nova Scotia, did not ask for relief. Not one cent of federal relief was paid in the province of Nova Scotia in those exceedingly difficult times. Now that a need, a definite, obvious and immediate need, has arisen, they deserve the very best consideration that can possibly be given to them.

". [DOT] . From an overwhelmingly agricultural country, Canada has been transformed into one of the great industrial countries of the world . . ."
